title: Shinhan Securities lifts GS E&C target on Korea AI data center, nuclear bets - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: Shinhan Investment & Securities said on the 16th that GS Engineering & Construction(006360) will see its earnings and valuation upgraded on the back of an expanded order pipeline that includes data centers and nuclear power plants. It raised its target price to 47,000 won from 38,000 won and maintained a "buy" (BUY) rating. The previous session's closing price was 37,800 won. Kim Seon-mi, a researcher at Shinhan Investment & Securities, said, "In the short term, the amount of AI data center orders and whether the U.S. nuclear Team Korea participates in orders will determine the upside potential for the share price," and added, "Although next year's results may fluctuate depending on the recognized order scale, earnings improvement will gradually take shape, supported by an expanded order pipeline from dwellings to data centers and nuclear power." Shinhan Investment & Securities estimated GS Engineering & Construction's revenue for next year at 11.81 trillion won and operating profit at 599.5 billion won. That represents growth of 7.4% and 5.5%, respectively, from this year's estimates. Kim said that if ground breaks on the Donghae AI data center (100MW), companywide results for next year and 2028 could be revised up by 3% to 5%. The project has passed the final review of the power system impact assessment and is under building permit review, with a goal to obtain approval in Sep. and break ground in Nov. Data centers will be the key variable for short-term results, given more than five non-group data center items in the pipeline (including Xi C&A). In addition, on a consolidation basis as of Sep., new presales at GS Engineering & Construction stand at 15,000 units, on track to exceed the annual plan. Kim noted that GS Engineering & Construction had a high share of presales in the first half of this year, which is expected to contribute to next year's revenue growth, and operating profit is likely to improve quickly from the second half of next year. As a key watchpoint for the second half of this year, the possibility of improving the financial structure through the sale of GS Inima was also mentioned. Kim said, "Despite the recent share price rise, the current PBR is around 0.6 times based on the current price, more than 20% discounted compared with competitors," adding, "The valuation gap will narrow depending on the construction schedules of major projects as they take shape."

title: "Which Moisturizer Should I Buy?"... GS Shop's AI Assists with Search, Reviews, and Comparison - 아시아경제

"Which Moisturizer Should I Buy?"... GS Shop's AI Assists with Search, Reviews, and Comparison Starting September 16, GS Shop will launch the 'AI Shopping Assistant' on its mobile app to help customers explore and select products. The AI Shopping Assistant is a service that applies AI technology to every stage of shopping, from product search and detailed information retrieval to review exploration and product comparison. Customers can ask and receive product-related questions in natural language through a conversational agent. It will first be applied to the beauty category and will be available through app updates released sequentially from September 16 to 20. Even if customers do not know the exact product name, they can search with everyday expressions during the search stage. For example, searching for 'moisture' prompts the AI to suggest relevant questions such as "Please recommend a moisture cream for dry skin" and "Is there a moisture cream that can be used for sensitive skin?" Customers can choose the question they are interested in and continue exploring. GS Shop will launch an 'AI Shopping Assistant' on its mobile app starting Wednesday, September 16, to help customers browse and select products. GS Shop On the product detail page, the 'AI Product Summary' provides a 3- to 4-line overview covering key features, ingredients, and texture. The 'AI Review Summary and Filter' summarizes frequently mentioned advantages and cautions found in customer reviews, and selectively shows reviews that are related to interests such as moisturizing power or dryness. The 'AI Product Comparison' feature allows users to compare prices, benefits, key ingredients, skin concerns, texture, and more by category. If customers develop questions while browsing, they can ask the conversational agent. The agent responds by considering both the product currently being viewed and the context of previous conversations, so there is no need to re-enter product information. For example, when viewing a retinol ampoule, a customer might first ask about how to use it and then follow up with questions like "How many times per week is appropriate for beginners?" or "Is it okay to use in the morning?" Heo Yooncheol, Head of AX Innovation at GS Retail Home Shopping BU, said, "Starting with beauty products, we plan to gradually expand the scope of AI to help customers understand products more easily and confidently choose what suits them," and added, "By seamlessly integrating AI into the entire shopping journey, we aim to deliver a differentiated shopping experience where customers receive assistance whenever they need it." © The Asia Business Daily. title: GS Rollercoaster Season Heads to The Brickyard - Sportscar365
content: Forty-four cars entered for penultimate round of IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge season… The IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge GS rollercoaster season continued at Virginia International Raceway’s flowing, technical 3.27-mile layout. The GS championship lead changed hands for the fourth time this year, while the run of poor results for the GS race winner in their next race continued. Heading into this week’s penultimate round of the season at Indianapolis Motor Speedway, Turner Motorsport regained the lead for the first time since Watkins Glen courtesy of a third-place finish for Dillon Machavern and Luca Mars in their No. 95 BMW M4 GT4 EVO. The No. 95 car has sat fourth, second or first through all eight races this year. It has led the standings by as much as 200 points (leaving Round 4 at Mid-Ohio) and trailed by as many as 140 points (in fourth, leaving Round 6 at Canadian Tire Motorsport Park). They’re now at the head of a BMW 1-2, with the ever-consistent Austin Krainz and Stevan McAleer 80 points behind in the No. 27 AutoTechnic Racing BMW with six top-10s in eight races. Previous leader Robert Noaker, who entered VIR 100 points ahead, now sits 100 points back in third in the No. 13 McCumbee McAleer Racing Ford Mustang GT4 after being on the receiving end of late-race contact at VIR that dropped him and new co-driver Finn Wiebelhaus to a season-worst 21st-place finish. While four other cars and drivers – Bryce Ward’s No. 57 Winward Racing Mercedes-AMG GT GT4, Caio Chaves’ No. 54 Panam Motorsport Toyota GR Supra GT4 EVO2, Michael Cooper and Moisey Uretsky’s No. 44 Ibiza Farm Motorsport McLaren Artura GT4 and Allen Patten and Trenton Estep’s No. 66 OORE (formerly YRB Racing) Aston Martin Vantage AMR GT4 Evo – remain within 300 points, they’re all going to need a banner Indianapolis race and issues for the top three cars to cut into the deficit. Cooper and Uretsky led a McLaren 1-2 in Indianapolis a year ago. The unfortunate “2026 GS winner curse” hit Patten and Estep, who followed up their Road America win with 22nd at VIR. It’s the third straight result of 21st or worse for the GS winner in their next race, after 21st and 28th place finishes for the No. 57 car at CTMP and No. 12 RAFA Racing Toyota at Road America. Stephen Cameron Racing’s No. 19 Ford Mustang GT4 with Greg Liefooghe and Sean Quinlan, now up to 12th in points, will hope to buck that trend in Indianapolis. TCR, meanwhile, could see Mason Filippi and Bryson Morris wrap the title a race early in their No. 33 Bryan Herta Autosport Hyundai Elantra N TCR. With a 260-point lead over teammates Denis Dupont and Preston Brown in the No. 76 Herta Hyundai, Filippi and Morris need to gain 90 points to reach the 350-point threshold that could put the title out of reach pending tiebreakers. They’ve delivered seven podiums in eight races, including two wins, and benefited as most of their competition had tough races at VIR. In the 31-car GS field, Christine Sloss returns for the first time since Sebring in the rebranded No. 10 RaceWife Racing Aston Martin she’ll share with Glenn McGee. CarBahn with Peregrine Racing’s rebuilt No. 39 BMW M4 GT4 EVO returns to action after Jeff Westphal and Sean McAlister missed VIR. As scheduled, the No. 43 Andretti Performance Porsche 718 GT4 RS Clubsport of Jarett Andretti and Gabby Chaves is back for its second start of the year. Jenson Brickley’s arrival in the No. 77 Stallion Motorsports with GOU CUPRA Leon VZ TCR alongside Celso Neto is one of two driver changes in the 13-car TCR grid, with Bruno Junqueira back once again in the No. 56 Baker Racing Audi RS3 LMS TCR. BHA’s No. 18 Hyundai of Harry Gottsacker and Lance Bergstein is due to resume after an incident in qualifying sidelined them pre-race at VIR. The No. 55 Gou Racing with Stallion Audi RS 3 LMS TCR is also back in action after missing VIR. Pilot Challenge competitors have two practice sessions Friday. They qualify Saturday morning before racing at 2:30 p.m. EST. Live flag-to-flag coverage airs on Peacock starting at 2:25 p.m. EST and also streams live, ad-free courtesy of Michelin, on IMSA’s official YouTube channel. Altzman, Evans to team up in expanded effort for McCumbee McAleer Racing... 2025 TCR Europe champion to join Celso Neto in Stallion's CUPRA Leon VZ TCR... title: Can the S&P 500 Rally as Treasury Yields Rise? - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. US stocks have historically struggled when the Federal Reserve begins a cycle of hiking rates. But equities tend to generate gains a year after interest rates start rising, according to Goldman Sachs Research. The S&P 500 has posted an average three-month decline of 2% at the start of seven hiking cycles over recent decades, Ben Snider, chief US equity strategist, writes in a report. But looking further out, the index has delivered an average 12-month gain of 9%, with positive returns in every episode except 2022. In addition, much of the increase in rates from a cycle of Fed hikes may already be reflected in yields: Interest-rate markets are already pricing multiple rate increases by the middle of 2027, making it less likely that monetary policy will produce a hawkish surprise for markets. "The medium-term impact of Fed tightening on equities will depend on how tightening affects earnings growth, which is the most important driver of stocks," Snider writes. Ten-year US Treasury yields have risen to about 5%, the highest since 2007. US core consumer price inflation in August was higher than consensus estimates, and our economists now expect the Federal Open Market Committee to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points this week. Goldman Sachs Research’s rate strategists believe that the combination of rising oil prices, a repricing of the Fed path, strong economic growth, and investment in artificial intelligence (AI) has lifted long-term interest rates. Equity multiples have declined this year, but valuations relative to bonds have been roughly unchanged. The S&P 500’s forward price-to-earnings ratio has dropped from 22x at the start of 2026 to 19x. While uncertainty around AI returns and questions about the staying power of recent earnings growth have contributed to that decline, rising interest rates have also been part of the story, according to Goldman Sachs Research. At the same time, the gap between the S&P 500 earnings yield (5.2%) and the real, inflation-adjusted 10-year Treasury yield (2.6%) is around 270 basis points. Outside of brief market selloffs, that spread—a simple proxy for the equity risk premium—has been fairly steady over the past two years, Snider writes. There is no consistent pattern for sector performance when the Fed starts increasing rates. Energy and technology companies have delivered the strongest average returns in the three months following an initial hike, while healthcare has posted the weakest average returns, according to Goldman Sachs Research. No sector has reliably outperformed or underperformed across past episodes of rate hikes. The sensitivity of US stocks to interest rates, meanwhile, varies widely. The valuations of "long-duration" stocks with high growth rates and low current profits are particularly vulnerable to rising yields. That’s because the cash flows underpinning their present values are concentrated in the distant future, Snider writes. In contrast, financial companies’ earnings and share prices tend to benefit when interest rates rise. Like the broader information technology sector, AI stocks have shown a modest negative correlation with real yields. Stocks involved in home construction are one of the most sensitive parts of the equity market to long-term interest rates. Housing stocks have traded in lockstep with bond yields during the past few months, underperforming the equal-weighted S&P 500 by 16 percentage points since June. It is not just the level of interest rates that matters—it is how fast they move, Snider writes. In recent decades, stocks have usually generated positive returns alongside rising interest rates unless the pace of the rate increase was more than two standard deviations above normal. Today, that threshold would equate to an increase in 10-year Treasury yields of roughly 50 basis points over a month or 30 basis points over two weeks. “The speed of the rate moves during the last few weeks helps explain why stocks struggled to digest those changes,” Snider writes. Stocks are also more sensitive to long-term rates than to short-term rates. Roughly 75% of the present value of the S&P 500 reflects cash flows 10 years or more in the future, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Mirroring the long-term nature of equity cash flows, S&P 500 returns have the strongest correlation with changes in long-term bond yields. Interest rates can affect corporate earnings and solvency as well as equity valuations, but those risks appear limited, Snider says. S&P 500 borrowing costs have increased during the last few years alongside higher bond yields, but the increase has been modest because most S&P 500 company debt carries fixed rates and long maturities. In addition, interest expenses remain small relative to strong profits. Smaller companies generally have weaker balance sheets and higher shares of floating-rate debt, making them more vulnerable to changes in interest rates. A company can maintain its valuation as interest rates rise if investors see it as less risky (a lower equity risk premium) or expect it to grow faster, according to Goldman Sachs Research. To fully offset the impact of a 1 percentage point increase in the cost of equity from today's levels, a company's expected long-term growth would need to increase by 2 percentage points. One way to boost growth is through investment in capital expenditures and research and development. Mergers and acquisitions, as well as spinoffs, are also among the ways for companies to improve their outlook for growth. This article is being provided for educational purposes only. title: Why Global Bond Yields Are Surging - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Government bond yields have surged to multi-decade highs across the US, UK, Germany, and Japan. George Cole, head of European Rates Strategy for Goldman Sachs Research, says there is a range of factors behind the bond sell-off—from swelling fiscal deficits and borrowing tied to investment in artificial intelligence (AI) to resilient economic growth and an energy-price shock. In this episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges, he also explains what could bring yields back down. Allison Nathan: Bond yields around the world have been rising for most of this year and have recently surged. So are interest rates settling into a new higher normal, or is this a temporary dislocation? I'm Allison Nathan, and this is Goldman Sachs Exchanges. To understand why bond markets are under pressure—giving rise to higher bond yields—I’m sitting down with my colleague George Cole, who leads European Rates Strategy for Goldman Sachs Research. George joins me today from London. George, welcome to the program. Allison Nathan: So, George, it's easy to look at the headlines and think this is just a US story. We've obviously seen concern about inflation here in the US. There's concern about spending levels. But this bond sell-off is really happening everywhere. Is that right? George Cole: Yeah. No, that's right. So, as you said, I sit over here in London. I look primarily at the European bond markets, in Germany, in the UK. But when we look at the US, when we look at markets like Japan, we would really think of these four as the major government bond markets, the major benchmarks for the global economy and global fixed income markets, and we're seeing all of these markets move higher in yield. We're at multi-decade highs as we read about in the financial press. We're seeing yields pressing higher across all of these economies, and it doesn't look obvious that there's a single driver or a single market that is really leading the sell-off or driving it over a long period of time. From day to day, one move might be bigger in one of those economies, but really over the last few months, all of those markets have been pushing yields higher. Allison Nathan: Well, that's my follow-up to you, George, because the question is what is driving this? And my intuition would be the rest of the world is just following the US lead, but you're saying that that may not be the case. Every country might be dealing with their own issues? George Cole: Yeah. So as a rate strategist and as an economist, we'd be looking at yield curves and bond markets to try to think about and find clues what is driving the move? We could look which economy might be driving it. As I said, you know, it's not that obvious that you can point to  just one of those major bond markets as driving the sell-off. You could look at things like the shape of the yield curve. Maybe it's the front end of interest rate curves that is moving. That would be associated with expectations around policy rates that might be on the move, maybe reflecting cyclical conditions, better growth, higher inflation. It could be maybe the long end of the curve is moving. That could be a term premia type of issue, the price of duration risk, maybe fiscal risks or maybe even long-term growth further out the curve. And what we're seeing across the yield curve is that all the way from the 30-year point on the curve, which has got a lot of attention and yields are much higher there than they have been in recent decades, but all the way down the 10-year point on the curve and even the policy rate expectations or pricing one or two years out is looking much higher, maybe not right at the peak of where we were in 2022, but certainly very high relative to where we've been in recent years. So, it looks like we've got broad-based pressure across a range of different factors. Allison Nathan: And so what are then the fundamental drivers, or are there not? What do you attribute all of this movement to? George Cole: I'm glad you asked are there fundamentals behind it, and this is one of the features of this sell-off I think it is a little underappreciated when you might read about it, is that actually the volatility of the moves have been relatively low. Now, of course, we're dealing with a revision right now of central bank expectations, and we're maybe moving toward an expectation that rates will be moving higher from central banks. That's now inducing a little bit of volatility in the market. But if we go back to, say, July, and think about the move since then in yields higher, what has been really striking is that volatility has been low, both the realized volatility of the market and also the price of volatility, the implied volatility that is priced into the market as well. Now, we might be a little bit higher in the range of the year, but If you look at on a multi-year horizon, volatility is actually quite low. And that feature of this sell-off makes it much harder to argue, well, this is a non-fundamental move. This is happening because of some sort of technical reason or a move in the market that has outsized volatility that is not sustainable. When volatility remains low, it is harder to make that conclusion. What I would say is that there is an overlapping set of fundamentals here that are driving yields up, and that goes all the way from long-running themes like large deficits, fiscal policy that is driving debt level to historic or recent highs. We've had that since the pandemic. Now, that's not always and everywhere a guide to what markets do, but when you combine that with something that is operating over the last few years, the borrowing associated with AI CapEx. As more and more of the AI CapEx is financed in debt markets, we are seeing there's some competition now for government borrowing. And then the final layer this year, we've actually had pretty resilient growth across major economies. And very locally, and this is driving some of the most recent volatility, we are seeing a renewed push higher in energy prices following the ongoing war in Iran that is the last kind of inflationary push that is worrying the market. Now, what those things are combining to do, we know we've got this backdrop of elevated government supply. We've now got competition from private sector issuance—just at the moment, that bond demand is weaker because of higher inflation and actually resilient growth in the economy. And all of those things combine, we think, fundamentally to push yields up. Allison Nathan: Right. But when I look at this list of factors, the most recent one, of course, has been the surge in energy prices. And so my question is why now when many of those factors have been sort of long in the market, long in coming? Is that your answer? It's energy, or it's still a question we're trying to answer. George Cole: The move very recently, so, if we think about the potential for Bank of England rate hikes or further ECB rate hikes, the potential for the Fed to hike, those things are more determined by the nearer-term inflation considerations, particularly in Europe, where we've got not only rising oil prices, but also European gas prices. This is creating a real headache for the inflation outlook in Europe. There's no doubt the surge from energy prices should prove temporary, but it feels like the central banks there now are running out of a bit of patience to deal with what should be temporary shocks, and are willing to take a little bit more action to safeguard inflation further down the line. So you're right. That is what is driving the latest round of interest rate movements, and they have been a bit more volatile. And certainly, when the central bank comes into play, that is when you do see a little bit more of a pickup in rates volatility. But that really hasn't been the story of the entire sell-off, not say if we rewind to something like July, the move has been more gradual, more orderly, and driven by the long end of the curve, which suggests some of these more longer running factors that you mentioned also are contributing. But I would certainly stress that it is the overlap and combination of these factors that I think gets us to where we are today. Allison Nathan: So the other major development in the recent period has been that the US Treasury has been engaged in bond buybacks. Tell us more about that and its implications. Why are they doing that? George Cole: Yeah. So the bond buybacks is a program that the US Treasury have had for some years now. The idea of the program is to, if you think about the bond market, the most liquid bonds that are out there in the system are the ones that have been issued recently. The bonds that have been issued some time ago are less liquid, there's less turnover in these bonds. And so the buyback program is designed to take some of those less liquid bonds out of the system and replace them with fresher bonds. So if you think about that motivation, it's kind of a liquidity operation. It just greases the bond market with these newer, fresher bonds. The announcement some weeks ago that we heard from the US Treasury that they would increase the size of buybacks at the long end of the curve, and the practical effect of that will be to reduce the maturity of the debt stock. You would be taking out some of these less liquid bonds, maybe over a 10- or 20- or 30-year maturity, and you would be replacing them with bonds that you're issuing usually at lower maturities, and maybe even using Treasury bills. And so, in effect, this is a switch to take longer maturity but less liquid bonds out of the system and replace them with shorter-maturity bonds. If we think about that in the context of what other Treasuries across the major economies, so the UK Debt Management Office, the DMO, is a good example of this. At the end of last year, the DMO announced that they would be reducing the amount of 30-year bonds that they would be issuing to the market, and that did have some effect to lower the yield in the 30-year part of the curve, but only on a relative basis. A little bit of a curve effect and a little bit of an effect to support 30-year yields lower against, say, swap rates. What it didn't do was change the macro price of the bond or the level of the yields, only really the fundamentals, expectations around policy, around fiscal policy, around inflation can do that. And again, the UK is a great example here. Despite the fact we haven't seen very many 30-year bonds issued recently, 30-year yields are still near the highs. And so in that sense, it's not going to change the macro fundamentals. Allison Nathan: Right, George but I do think the market interpretation of this announcement, which I think was somewhat unexpected, please correct me if I'm wrong, was that this was an attempt by the Treasury to reduce long-end yields. But you don't think it will have that effect, setting their motivations aside, that's not your observation. George Cole: Yeah. So I think that the announcement came in an unanticipated way. It was not in the regular schedule of the communication of the US Treasury to the market via its refunding announcements. And so in that sense, there was initially a bit of ambiguity about exactly what the program was designed to achieve. Part of the rationale subsequently was that there would be some attempt to improve liquidity at the long end of the curve. And again, following the pattern that we're seeing in the other debt management offices or the other Treasuries and issuers across sovereign markets, it does seem a very natural thing to try to balance the supply and demand dynamics across the yield curve. There are deficits to finance, and the Treasury in the US and elsewhere need to make a decision, how do we finance that? What's the optimal way to issue that debt? Well, when we have a situation where yields are high, central banks are no longer buying debt, we've got reduced demand from, say, pension funds, other investors that typically buy these longer-dated bonds. There's lower demand because at these higher yield levels, liabilities of, say, pension systems that are being discounted at these higher levels of rates, they are now much lower. And so that demand has actually fallen despite the fact yields have moved higher. And that means that Treasuries and issuers, it makes a lot of sense to think about lowering the amount of longer-dated issuance, and relying on more liquid and lower and shorter maturities, and that's exactly what we've seen across a number of economies. So if we view that as the pattern that we're seeing across across these sovereign issuers, then this increased buybacks at the long-end is just a different way to do that. You could reduce auction sizes, or you could do these buybacks to get these longer-dated bonds out of the market. In the end the effect will be the same. But I certainly would say the evidence across whether it's the UK, Japan to some extent has made some steps to reduce long-end issuance, that's not really doing much to change the macro price. And we are seeing yields in those markets very much being determined by the deeper fundamentals. Are there worries about inflation or fiscal risks? Are there issuance pressures that are maybe outside of governments that are also leading to those higher yields? Those are the things that are really going determine the level of yields. Allison Nathan: Understood. Let's get back again to some of these drivers of these long-term bond yields reaching higher levels. We talked about the US dealing with really an unprecedented deficit outside of war times, but there's also rising regional tensions that are forcing Europe and Asia to spend heavily on their own defense. So, we are seeing sort of fiscal pressures globally. Does that really mean, again, just coming back to the drivers, that higher rates are just really simply the cost or maybe the permanent cost of today's fiscal and to some extent even geopolitical realities? George Cole: Yeah. So, I think that when we look at the fiscal outlook, what you really want to be paying attention to are what are the non-discretionary elements of the budget spending that are committed to. Entitlement spending, obviously a big one and has importance across all of the major economies and interest costs, and this is something as we keep rolling over government debt at these higher levels of yields, this is a non-negotiable cost that governments need to pay. So, there is pressure on budgets from that source. And if you add on that commitments to increase defense spending, which as you mentioned, across a number of geographies, but certainly here in Europe, that is a commitment that you're increasingly seeing governments make, the UK being a great example of that. It does lead to very challenging budget choices. You need to think, how will that additional spending be financed when the budget's already under pressure? It could be via higher revenue, higher taxation. It could be via reduced spending elsewhere, or it could be by renewed borrowing. And so that's why the bond market is watching fiscal events and wants to understand exactly what priorities governments will be giving. Of course, we're also in a situation where there is a competition for savings, and I mentioned before, we've got a situation where the private sector is undertaking a very significant uplift of CapEx. Borrowing is being used to finance that. And so just at the moment where governments are attempting this uplift in some areas of spending, there is now a competition for savings. And if we think about what that does to the savings investment balance globally, we have fewer savings, we have more investment, and the way to clear that market is by raising interest rates. So, it may not be here forever, but it certainly is an environment where at the moment, while those spending pressures or spending commitments are under pressure to expand and there's a competition for those global savings, we should expect that higher rates are part of the environment. Allison Nathan: Right. Let's zoom out for a moment, George. I'm looking at the screen at over 5% 10-year US yields. That seems so high to me. But if you really think about history, that was much closer to the pre-global financial crisis norm. So, in some sense, is this really just a return to a normal, potentially even healthier environment? George Cole: Yeah, so if you look at the long time series of yields, you're absolutely right. We haven't seen these levels for many decades, maybe in some cases. But if you look at the longer history of yields, the levels that we're at are not all that unusual, and I think consistent with some of the big shifts that we've seen, say, over the last five years or so. The most obvious one is the big shift higher in both the level and the distribution of inflation risk. That, if you compare that to where we were in the decade following the global financial crisis into the pandemic, couldn't be more different. That was when we were worried about weakness in demand, very weak inflation outcomes. Policy couldn't quite generate the inflation re-pressure that it wanted to, and so the distribution of risks in the bond market was to lower yields. Now we have a distribution of inflation outcomes that looks maybe even more than higher than central bank targets but certainly much more symmetric around central bank targets. And in some sense, that connects us back to something looks a little more normal, relative to the decade following the global financial crisis. There is one big difference, which is fiscal positions are different to where they were back in a period where yields were higher, both nominal yields and real yields. We now have much bigger debt burdens. We have bigger deficits. So that is something that is much more part of the discussion. Can you have a normal yield environment this high with fiscal policy as it is currently struck? One of the ways I think you can delay answering that question is high nominal growth as long as growth both on the real side, but if you also have a cushion of inflation is higher, that is something that can sustain yields at these levels. But those are the questions for the future. How will we bear the rise in interest costs that the current yield curve would imply? And then maybe when I think about some specific markets, somewhere like Germany, the German yield curve is not yet back to levels that we saw pre-global financial crisis. There are good reasons for that, I think, as we learned through not only the GFC, but then the European sovereign crisis. The rise of credit spreads in European sovereign markets does create a little bit of a more challenging environment to sustain much higher bund yields. If you have high bund yields plus a credit spread to other sovereign markets in Europe, that creates much tighter financial conditions for borrowing in some of those other economies. And so, there is something that is probably going to keep the distribution of German yields a little lower. On the flip side of that, we're seeing maybe now the prospect of something like sustainable 2% or something close to it in Japan in inflation, and that's something we haven't seen for several decades. And so it does look like Japanese yields might be at a higher end of the range relative to they've in recent decades. Allison Nathan: But if you think about the forward, George, what are you expecting in terms of rates? Will they remain at these elevated levels? Where do we go from here? George Cole: Yeah, so going back to one of the things we mentioned before, this sell-off is broad, it's been across the curve, it's been across economies. And although we are maybe now witnessing something that looks a little bit more volatile as central banks come into play, generally it's been a relatively low-vol sell-off. That tells you that there are probably fundamental views in the market behind the sell-off. So, my view is it's going to take a fundamental to beat a fundamental, and so if you want to get yields lower, you've got to have some sort of pathway to lower inflation, I think is the most obvious way to think about what would get yields lower. The proximate source of that, if you wanted to think about a reversal of what's driving yields higher in the very short run, is global energy prices. So both the oil market, refined products, the European gas market. That is really difficult to have a lot of conviction on in the near term, given its link to the geopolitical events, the war in Iran, and so near-term visibility is really hard. On a six to 12-month basis, our commodity strategists do expect at some point these commodity markets are likely to be better supplied and see those prices come down. So are we still worried about energy price inflation in six to 12 months' time? We hope not. We forecast not. That would be one way to get lower yields, particularly in the front end of the curve, where central banks don't need to quite be as worried as maybe the market thinks they will be about the energy price inflation. And then over the longer run, I think an interesting one is to think about what happens to this AI investment cycle. And at some point, you would imagine that investment needs will decrease once the investments begin to bear fruit. And one of the questions for the rates markets is, can you seamlessly go from the borrowing phase to the implementation phase where we transition into this world of higher growth and higher productivity? That might include a higher cost of capital further down the line. But to the extent there's any bumps in that journey, if investment expectations were to fall, if there was some sort of other growth shock that could see a revision of some of those expectations, if there's maybe some of the disinflationary impacts of AI productivity growth that happen a little faster than expected, that would be the other way that you could imagine some of the pressure that we're seeing in the bond market is alleviated. And so, in that sense, those seem to me to be both in the near term and the more medium term, the most plausible drivers. Of course, we'd be watching things like fiscal policy very closely, and if you do see a move toward fiscal tightening or something changes in the fiscal trajectory, that would be also something as a sign for lower yields. But as it stands, I think near term, energy prices, that's what's delivering a lot of the near-term movement and volatility in markets, and then the forward trajectory of the AI CapEx cycle is really the key thing to watch. Allison Nathan: So still a lot of uncertainty, of course, around all of those factors. So, what would be your key takeaway, George, for investors right now? Should they be reevaluating the duration of risk profiles within their portfolios or just see how this evolves and hold tight? George Cole: In the very near term, the risk to bonds is coming from the energy markets, and then I think most importantly, the connection to central bank pricing where central banks, they just run out of road. They can't tolerate the inflation anymore, and they need to hike. That would be the most plausible proximate risk that would manifest in the front end, and that would be an environment where the yield curve would flatten. In that situation, you probably would see a decline in growth expectations, maybe inflation expectations further out the curve. That wouldn't necessarily see longer term yields a lot higher. You might see stability out in the forward curve. And if we think about that then in combination with the broader investment outlook whether it's the equity market or credit markets, a huge amount of connection to the AI investment theme, that is when you can maybe start to build a portfolio where bonds have some hedge value, where if we find that the AI CapEx trajectory, undershoots expectations or that there is some sort of disinflationary impact that comes faster than expected and rates need to move lower, that is when you can start to build a case that although it's very uncertain what happens in the next three months, maybe yields are a little higher, certainly if we don't see any energy relief. If you start to think about the distribution of outcomes over a two, three, four-year horizon, it may start to be a little bit more asymmetric for the five-year yield part of the curve where yields can move lower and start to hedge some of the exposure that are in global investment portfolios. Allison Nathan: Thanks, George, for your insights. Happy to have you here. Allison Nathan: This episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges was recorded on Monday, September 14th, 2026. content: The Dow and Nasdaq Composite each fell 0.7% by midday while the S&P 500 held up better at a 0.4% loss. Chip stocks reversed Monday's selloff, with Qualcomm up 4% and Advanced Micro Devices gaining 2.3%. The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.041%, its highest level since July 2007. Yesterday the market was worried about artificial intelligence. Today it went back to worrying about interest rates, which have a much longer track record. The Dow Jones Industrial Average(DJINDICES: ^DJI) dropped 0.7% as of 1:16 p.m. ET, with the Nasdaq Composite(NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) matching it. The S&P 500(SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) took a lighter hit, falling 0.4%. Only seven of the Dow's 30 stocks posted gains at this checkpoint. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.041% on Tuesday morning, a level not seen since July 2007. Oil kept pushing in the same direction. Brent crude rose 2.6% to $108.41 and U.S. crude added 3.3% to $104.76 while traders tried to figure out how long Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline stays offline. Someone will be wrong, and real-world oil prices will eventually set the record straight. The United States Oil Fund(NYSEMKT: USO) gained 4.1% today. Monday's AI panic mostly unwound. title: 10 Luxury Cars That Won't Drain Your Wallet On Repairs - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update Luxury cars are supposed to make ownership feel effortless. They typically offer quieter cabins, better materials, stronger performance, and more technology than ordinary cars, but there is usually a catch: When something eventually goes wrong, the bill can quickly take some of the shine off the premium ownership experience. That does not mean every luxury car is destined to drain its owner's bank account. Some premium models combine sophisticated interiors and impressive driving experiences with powertrains that have proven capable of keeping repair costs relatively manageable. Others have strong reliability records that make them particularly appealing as long-term purchases. The luxury cars listed here highlight 10 models that won't drain their owners' bank accounts, based on Edmunds maintenance and repair cost estimates over 5 years, giving buyers a useful starting point when looking for a premium vehicle that won't turn every trip to the repair shop into a financial emergency. J.D. Power reliability ratings provide another useful piece of the puzzle. Its Quality & Reliability score measures owner-reported defects, malfunctions, and design flaws, with higher scores indicating fewer problems. The result is a lineup that proves luxury and reliability do not always have to be mutually exclusive. The Lexus ES has long occupied an interesting position in the luxury sedan market. It offers the comfort, quietness, and premium appointments buyers expect from a luxury car without relying on the most complicated mechanical formula in the segment. The ES 300h is particularly interesting because its hybrid powertrain, which produces a modest 215 horsepower and 163 lb-ft of torque, can deliver strong fuel economy while avoiding some of the mechanical complexity associated with high-output turbocharged engines. The combination of a naturally aspirated 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, electric motors, and a continuously variable transmission (CVT) is designed more around smoothness and efficiency than outright performance. That makes the ES 300h a particularly sensible choice for someone who wants to move into luxury ownership without embracing an expensive performance-oriented powertrain. J.D. Power's 2025 Lexus ES data gives the model an overall consumer score of 83 out of 100 and, more importantly, a Great Quality & Reliability score of 89/100. Looking more closely at the ES 300h F SPORT Handling trim, this model has an impressively low estimated maintenance and repair cost of just $4,564 over 5 years, with $3,728 attributed to maintenance and the remaining $836 covering repairs. These figures don't mean an owner will never face an expensive repair, nor do they guarantee that every example will cost exactly this amount. Vehicle age, mileage, maintenance history and condition can all have a major effect on actual ownership costs. Still, when a luxury sedan combines a relatively modest Edmunds estimate with a strong J.D. Power reliability score, it becomes difficult to ignore. The Volvo V60 T8 Polestar Engineered takes a very different approach to luxury than the Lexus ES. Instead of prioritizing relaxed cruising above everything else, Volvo gives this wagon serious performance credentials. Its plug-in hybrid powertrain combines a turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine with electric assistance, while the Polestar Engineered specification adds performance-focused hardware and tuning. This variant's plug-in hybrid arrangement develops 455 horsepower and 523 lb-ft of torque and is paired with an eight-speed automatic transmission. It's the sort of car that can serve as a practical family wagon during the week while still providing considerably more excitement when the road opens up. That combination makes its relatively low position on this list particularly interesting. J.D. Power's 2025 V60 Cross Country data gives the broader V60 family an overall consumer score of 77/100 and a Quality & Reliability score of 77/100, rated Average. The rating isn't as impressive as the Lexus models on this list, but it does show why reliability should be considered alongside, rather than instead of, ownership cost. The V60 has an estimated Edmunds maintenance and repair cost of $4,783, including $3,142 for maintenance and $1,641 for repairs, putting it only slightly behind the Lexus ES. That is notable considering the Volvo's sophisticated plug-in hybrid system and performance-oriented specification. Buyers should still remember that newer vehicles have less long-term reliability history available, so the low estimate should not be interpreted as a guarantee of trouble-free ownership. Nevertheless, for someone who wants a luxury wagon with genuine performance credentials, the V60 T8 makes an intriguing case. The Acura MDX has built its reputation around being the sensible alternative to more expensive European luxury SUVs. It offers three-row practicality, premium equipment, and a strong 3.5-liter V6 powerplant that makes 290 horsepower and 267 lb-ft of torque, coupled with a 10-speed automatic transmission, giving the three-row SUV plenty of power without straying too far from the mechanical simplicity of a conventional gasoline SUV. That formula has made the MDX particularly appealing to families who want luxury without giving up everyday practicality. J.D. Power's rating varies by model year, but the 2024 MDX receives an overall score of 80/100 and a Great Quality & Reliability rating of 83/100. The 2025 model, meanwhile, carries a 77/100 Quality & Reliability score. The MDX's $4,978 Edmunds maintenance and repair estimate breaks down at $4,171 for maintenance and only $807 for repairs, which keeps it comfortably below the $5,000 mark over a 5-year period. That is a meaningful figure for a luxury three-row SUV. Bigger vehicles can bring bigger bills simply because they have more equipment and larger components, but the MDX demonstrates that premium family transportation doesn't automatically require premium repair spending. For buyers who need space but don't want to sacrifice reliability or reasonable ownership costs, the MDX is one of the strongest all-rounders here. The Infiniti Q50 is proof that a luxury sedan doesn't have to look conservative to make financial sense. Its twin-turbocharged V6 produces a healthy 300 horsepower and 295 lb-ft of torque and sends power to the rear wheels via a seven-speed automatic transmission, giving it considerably more attitude than the typical comfort-focused luxury sedan. At the same time, the cabin offers the premium environment buyers expect from Infiniti. The important factor here is that the Q50 has been around long enough for its reliability record to become easier to evaluate. For 2021, J.D. Power gave the Q50 an overall consumer score of 80/100 and a Great Quality & Reliability score of 81/100. The 2020 Q50 also ranked fourth in its J.D. Power compact premium car category with an overall score of 81/100, although its Quality & Reliability category was not rated for that particular year's data. At $8,089, the Q50 marks the point where the estimated ownership costs begin to climb considerably. Of the latter figure, $6,007 is attributed to maintenance, while repairs are estimated at $2,082 over 5 years. That doesn't necessarily make it a bad buy. The Q50 delivers respectable performance, and used examples can be considerably more accessible than some German competitors. The key is finding a well-maintained example. A luxury car with a strong maintenance history can be dramatically more appealing than a cheaper example that has been neglected. The 2020 Acura TLX sits in a sweet spot for buyers who want an affordable entry into used luxury ownership. Its 2.4-liter four-cylinder gasoline engine produces 206 horsepower and 182 lb-ft of torque, while the front-wheel-drive configuration sends power through Acura's automatic transmission. The smaller engine is less intimidating than some of the larger powerplants available in the luxury segment, while the TLX itself provides a comfortable and well-equipped cabin. It also avoids the badge premium attached to some of its German rivals. J.D. Power gave the 2020 TLX an overall score of 79/100, with a Great Quality & Reliability rating of 81/100. It also ranked third in the Midsize Premium Car category that year. The estimated Edmunds maintenance and repair cost comes to $8,181 for the front-wheel-drive derivative powered by the firm's 2.4-liter four-cylinder gas engine. The over-$8,000 estimate is split between $5,459 for maintenance and $2,722 for repairs. While that is not necessarily cheap in absolute terms, it is still more affordable than what buyers might face with some European luxury rivals or the higher TLX trim levels that use the more powerful 3.5-liter 6-cylinder engine. Opting for all-wheel drive also pushes the estimated maintenance and repair cost even higher. The TLX's appeal, then, is that buyers can get a premium sedan with a strong reliability record without necessarily stepping into the potentially higher repair exposure associated with some European alternatives. It is also an example of why reliability should not be judged purely by the size of a repair estimate. A car can cost more to maintain over a long period while still being fundamentally dependable. The Lexus IS 350 is one of the most compelling cars on this list because it manages to combine reliability with genuine driver appeal. Its naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 churns out 311 horsepower and 280 lb-ft of torque and is paired with a six-speed automatic transmission in this all-wheel-drive configuration, forming a major part of the attraction. Instead of depending on forced induction to produce its power, the engine uses a relatively straightforward formula that has become familiar across the Lexus and Toyota family. The result is a sports sedan that doesn't require buyers to choose between fun and long-term dependability. J.D. Power's 2021 Lexus IS data gives the model a Great Quality & Reliability score of 88/100, along with an overall consumer score of 86/100. The 2024 IS achieves a Quality & Reliability score of 88/100. The Lexus IS 350's Edmunds estimate comes to $8,202, with the majority of that figure ($7,246) going toward maintenance and just $956 attributed to repairs. That puts it almost level with the TLX, but the IS has an advantage for buyers who want something with more enthusiast appeal. Its combination of a naturally aspirated V6, available all-wheel drive, and Lexus's reputation for durability makes it one of the more convincing performance-luxury choices here. It is not the cheapest car to maintain on this list, but it offers something that is arguably more important: a compelling reason to own it beyond simply wanting a luxury badge. Front three-quarter shot of a black 2023 Lexus RX driving on a highway The Lexus NX 300h takes the ES formula and packages much of it into the increasingly popular luxury crossover format. The hybrid powertrain combines a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine with electric assistance and a CVT for a total system output of 194 horsepower, while the F SPORT Black Line specification gives the compact SUV a more distinctive appearance. For buyers who want an upscale SUV but don't necessarily need the size of an RX or MDX, the NX is a logical middle ground. J.D. Power gives the 2021 Lexus NX an overall score of 83/100 and a Great Quality & Reliability score of 88/100. It also ranked second in the Compact Premium SUV category and was recognized with a J.D. Power Dependability Award. The Edmunds maintenance and repair estimate is $9,634, with maintenance accounting for $6,394 and repairs estimated at $3,240 for the NX 300h SUV F SPORT Black Line. Although this is considerably higher than the ES 300h's figure, the NX demonstrates why a maintenance estimate should not be confused with a reliability score. J.D. Power's 88/100 Quality & Reliability rating is strong, suggesting that owners generally experienced relatively few problems even though long-term maintenance and repair expenses can still accumulate. For someone searching specifically for a reliable luxury SUV, that distinction matters. The Lexus LS 500 is the wild card on this list. This isn't simply an entry-level luxury sedan trying to compete with mainstream vehicles. The LS is Lexus's flagship sedan, built to take on cars such as the Mercedes-Benz S-Class, BMW 7 Series and Audi A8. The entry-level LS 500 is powered by a twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V6 gasoline engine producing 416 horsepower and 442 lb-ft of torque, mated with a 10-speed automatic transmission. Yet Lexus has historically positioned the LS around refinement and engineering quality rather than excessive mechanical drama. J.D. Power describes the 2025 LS as combining luxury, performance, build quality, reliability and resale value while competing against those established European flagships. That makes the LS particularly interesting for buyers who want genuine flagship luxury but are nervous about the ownership costs associated with it. With an Edmunds maintenance and repair estimate of $9,752, the LS is certainly not cheap to own. The majority of the latter figure is attributed to maintenance ($8,778), while repairs are estimated at a much more palatable $1,007. But consider what that money buys. This is a full-size flagship luxury sedan with a twin-turbocharged V6, extensive technology and a cabin designed to compete with the most prestigious vehicles in the world. The fact that it can appear on a list focused on avoiding punishing repair bills says something about Lexus's approach to luxury engineering. The Lexus GS may no longer be in production, but that could make the 2020 GS 350 even more interesting to used-car shoppers. It represents an era when Lexus was still producing a traditional rear-wheel-drive luxury sedan with a naturally aspirated V6. The GS 350 combined comfort with much stronger driving dynamics than the stereotypical luxury cruiser. The 3.5-liter V6 is also one of the reasons the GS has developed such a strong reputation among Lexus enthusiasts. The 2020 Lexus GS 350 F SPORT Black Line features a 3.5-liter V6 engine producing 311 horsepower and 218 lb-ft of torque, mated to an eight-speed automatic transmission with rear-wheel drive. J.D. Power's GS data has historically been particularly strong. The 2015 GS, for example, earned an 89/100 Quality & Reliability score, rated Great, and won a J.D. Power Dependability Award. Edmunds maintenance cost is estimated at $7,027, while repairs are estimated at $2,824 over 5 years for the 2020 GS 350 F SPORT Black Line. This adds up to an estimated maintenance and repair bill of $9,851, placing the GS near the top of this list. Again, that does not mean a GS is inherently unreliable. Rather, the figure reflects the cumulative cost of maintaining and repairing a luxury vehicle over its ownership period. For a buyer willing to shop carefully for a well-maintained example, the GS 350's blend of naturally aspirated V6 power, traditional luxury-sedan proportions and Lexus reliability makes it one of the more interesting used luxury cars available. The Lexus RX is arguably the most mainstream luxury SUV on this list, but that does not make it any less compelling. The RX has spent decades establishing itself as a comfortable alternative to European luxury SUVs. Its formula is relatively simple: a quiet and comfortable cabin, plenty of technology, an upscale driving experience, and the sort of reliability that makes long-term ownership less stressful. The 2025 Lexus RX 350 F SPORT Design features a turbocharged 2.4-liter four-cylinder engine producing 275 horsepower and 317 lb-ft of torque, coupled with an eight-speed automatic transmission. J.D. Power's 2025 RX data gives the SUV an overall score of 81/100 and a Great Quality & Reliability score of 82/100. Previous generations have also performed strongly, with the 2022 RX earning an 88/100 Quality & Reliability score. The RX finishes this list with an Edmunds maintenance and repair estimate of $9,975. Of the latter figure, maintenance is estimated at $8,968, while repairs account for $1,007 over 5 years. That makes it the most expensive vehicle here according to Edmunds estimated figures, but it is important not to interpret that as the RX being the least reliable. In fact, its J.D. Power scores tell a different story. The RX continues to receive strong reliability marks, showing that projected long-term maintenance costs and the likelihood of experiencing defects are not the same measurement. For buyers who want a luxury SUV that can serve as a daily family vehicle for years, the RX remains a particularly strong proposition. We want to hear from you. title: Liberia G S Yogaga attack: Ghana Navy commemorates 36th anniversary - Ghana News Agency
content: Ghana's preferred news source: Accurate, Credible, Objective, Timely Africans& Diaspora Sekondi (W/R), Sept. 15, GNA – The Ghana Navy has held a Memorial Day Anniversary Parade in remembrance of its heroes who paid the ultimate price in the bombing of the Ghana Navy Ship (GNS) Yogaga in Liberia 36 years ago.   Journalism& News Industry The religious parade, marked by a wreath-laying ceremony at the Western Naval Command Cenotaph, was also to honour the memories of all the brave men and women of the Navy, and the Ghana Armed Forces in general, who laid down their lives in their line of duties both home and abroad. The 36th anniversary parade of the bombing of the GNS Yogaga, held at the Sekondi Naval Base Ceremonial Jetty, was attended by government officials, senior officers, heads of sister security agencies, senior and junior ratings, families of fallen soldiers, traditional leaders, retired officers, and students among others. Mr Fredrick F. Faidoo, the Sekondi-Takoradi Metropolitan Chief (MCE), who represented the Western Regional Minister at the event, said the sacrifices of the officers and sailors who fell during the attack on GNS Yogaga in Liberia, and all other soldiers who gave their lives in the line of duty, stood as a lasting testament to the courage, loyalty, and devotion to duty which defined the traditions of the Ghana Armed Forces.   Africans& Diaspora He noted that the remembrance was more than a ceremonial obligation, but also a national responsibility, adding that a nation that honoured its heroes preserved its history, strengthened its values and inspired future generations. He said: “As we reflect on the sacrifices of the past, we must also consider the responsibility that rests upon us today, because the greatest tribute we can pay to our fallen heroes is to live by the values they exemplified, and their courage, loyalty and devotion to duty must continue to inspire us in our service to the nation and in our daily lives.” Mr Faidoo acknowledged the vital roles of the Ghana Navy in safeguarding the country’s peace and security, and its maritime domain. He commended the officers, sailors and defence civilian staff of the Ghana Navy for their commitment to duty, noting that despite the complex security challenges that continued to confront the Gulf of Guinea, Ghana’s maritime domain remained one of the most secured in the sub-region. He, however, said the government recognised the challenges under which the personnel operated, and gave the assurance the authorities would continue to put in place measures to support them to enhance their operational efficiency. Commodore Stephen Billins Nyam, the Flag Officer Commanding (FOC) the Western Naval Command, said the anniversary parade served as an opportunity for them to renew their pledge to uphold the ideals and values for which the fallen heroes laid down their lives. He said: “The men we honour today were ordinary men who answered an extraordinary call when duty demanded it of them, and like many of us, they carried hopes for the future and personal aspirations, while their loved ones waited for their safe return from various duties and missions. For the great price they paid, their memory and legacy of sacrifice must never be forgotten.” He encouraged current personnel to be inspired by the sacrifices and legacies of the fallen heroes, and continue uphold the ideals of courage, discipline, professionalism, and loyalty that defined the Ghana Navy. The Ghana Navy has set aside September 14 each year to commemorate the life and achievements of fallen comrades, who were assigned to end a civil war in Liberia, where a group of West African Nations under the auspices of ECOWAS took steps to send peacekeeping Force to Monrovia in August 1990. The Force was known as the Economic Community of West Africa Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) with troops drawn from Ghana, Nigeria, Sierra-Leone, Gambia, Guinea, Burkina Faso, and Niger where the Ghana Navy contributed two ships namely; GNS Achimota and GNS Yogaga, as part of the Task Force. On September 14, 1990, the GNS Yogaga was attacked by a faction involved in the civil war killing three crew members of the ship on the spot. In all, 15 ECOMOG personnel lost their lives and others sustained injuries. Similarly, several naval personnel paid the ultimate price on internal and external operations in the pursuit of global peace and security. title: GS Caltex Marks 22nd Year of Chuseok Giving in Yeosu - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
Support Reaches 128 Welfare Facilities and 700 Vulnerable Households
Local Seafood Added to Broaden Regional Partnership YEOSU — "It added warmth to the Chuseok table and vitality to local seafood." Ahead of the Chuseok holiday, GS Caltex once again delivered its annual gifts to Yeosu, a city in Jeonnam-Gwangju Integrated Metropolitan City. GS Caltex said it held the "2026 Chuseok Sharing of Warmth with GS Caltex" event on the 15th at Exhibition Hall D of the International Pavilion at the Yeosu Expo site. The gifts this year are worth 130 million won. Attending the event were Yeosu Mayor Seo Yeong-hak, Yeosu City Council Chair Ju Jae-hyeon, Jeong Cheol-seop, chair of the Yeosu Community Social Security Council, Jin Ki-seop, head of GS Caltex's facilities plant, and Kim Ki-eung, head of the company's SHE and external cooperation office. About 70 officials from local welfare facilities and volunteers also took part. Ten members of the GS Caltex employee volunteer corps and Hansothoe, an association of the company's retirees, helped package the goods. This year, GS Caltex is delivering 934 bags of 20-kilogram white rice, worth about 50 million won, to 128 social welfare facilities in the Yeosu area. It is also providing holiday food packages worth about 40 million won to a total of 700 households, including 600 low-income vulnerable households and 100 households of North Korean defectors. The packages contain glass noodles, thin wheat noodles, pancake mix, white sugar, beef bone broth, spicy beef soup, soy sauce, instant rice and sesame oil — items needed both for preparing holiday meals and for everyday cooking. This year's giving also carried a message of regional partnership. GS Caltex arranged support for seafood produced in Yeosu to cheer on the successful hosting of the 2026 Yeosu World Island Expo and to help boost the local economy. "We are grateful to GS Caltex for looking after neighbors in need in our community and sharing the warmth of the holidays every single year for 22 years," Mayor Seo said. "This year is all the more meaningful because we are also delivering local seafood, carrying our wish for the successful hosting of the Yeosu World Island Expo." "We have been able to continue sharing this warmth with an unchanging heart since 2005 because of the trust and support of the local community," said Jin, head of the facilities plant. "This seafood support offers practical help to vulnerable groups while also promoting consumption of local seafood, which carries the meaning of mutual growth." GS Caltex's "Chuseok Sharing of Warmth" program began in 2005 and has continued for 22 years, making it a signature holiday giving activity in the Yeosu area. Through this year, the company has delivered more than 1.9 billion won in goods and donations to the local community. Original reporting by Park Ji-hoon for Seoul Economic Daily. title: GS Construction Utilizes Augmented Reality (AR) in Quality Inspections for Enhanced Efficiency and Accuracy - 아시아경제
content:
GS Construction Utilizes Augmented Reality (AR) in Quality Inspections for Enhanced Efficiency and Accuracy GS Construction is enhancing the efficiency and accuracy of plant equipment quality inspections by leveraging augmented reality (AR) technology. GS Engineering & Construction is conducting quality inspections of plant equipment using augmented reality (AR) technology. GS Engineering & Construction On September 15, GS Construction announced that it will digitalize quality inspections by introducing “Twyn,” a digital inspection solution from German AR specialist company Visometry, to plant sites. The system allows inspectors to compare and inspect 3D design models with actual fabricated equipment before installation at the site. For plant construction, equipment undergoes quality inspections to verify whether the fabricated product matches the design drawings before being installed on site. Traditionally, inspectors would compare the drawings and the fabricated items manually, a process that was time-consuming for complex equipment. Additionally, discrepancies during inspection could arise depending on the inspector’s proficiency. Moreover, if quality anomalies are not detected during the manufacturing stage, additional rework may be required during the installation process at the site. To improve work efficiency in quality inspections, GS Construction adopted the “Twyn” digital inspection solution. The incorporation of “geometry-based automatic alignment and tracking” technology—capable of automatically matching 3D designs to equipment positions and orientations—enables usage even indoors where securing satellite signals is difficult. Inspectors first check for any major quality anomalies, such as missing components, incorrect installation, or incorrect position or orientation. For areas requiring further verification, a 3D laser scanner is used to precisely measure the actual shape, which is then compared to design standards for a more detailed inspection. GS Construction has applied AR-based quality inspections at four ongoing domestic and overseas plant sites. Based on the accumulated technology and operational experience from this process, the company plans to expand the application to areas such as steel modular construction and other manufacturing fields requiring repetitive quality checks. Going forward, GS Construction aims to systematically collect and manage inspection results and quality history data, continuously advancing the digitalization of quality inspection processes. A GS Construction official stated, “The biggest advantage is the ability to quickly identify quality anomalies by directly comparing the 3D design model to the fabricated product on site and to select items that require detailed inspection,” adding, “We will actively utilize digital technology to enhance the efficiency and reliability of plant quality management work.” © The Asia Business Daily. title: GS Engineering & Construction deploys AR to streamline plant quality inspections - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: GS Engineering & Construction will use Augmented Reality (AR) technology to improve the efficiency and accuracy of quality inspections for plant equipment and materials. GS Engineering & Construction said on the 15th that it will pursue the digitalization of quality inspections by introducing Visometry's digital inspection solution "Twyn" to plant sites and comparing and inspecting 3D design models with actual fabricated equipment and materials before on-site installation. Equipment and materials used in plant construction undergo a quality inspection before on-site installation to confirm that the design drawings match the actual fabricated items. Previously, inspectors mainly compared design drawings with fabricated items directly, which took considerable time for equipment and materials with complex structures and risked inconsistencies in the verification process depending on the inspector's level of experience. If quality issues are not detected during fabrication, additional rework may be required during installation, making swift and accurate inspections before installation critical. GS Engineering & Construction introduced the digital inspection solution "Twyn" to improve the efficiency of such quality inspection tasks. Twyn uses Augmented Reality (AR) technology to overlay and compare 3D design information with the actual fabricated item. Using a tablet, inspectors can compare the design model with the actual fabrication on site to verify fabrication status and consistency with design information. In particular, it applies a "shape-based automatic alignment and tracking" technology that automatically matches the position and orientation of the 3D design and the equipment and materials. Unlike AR methods that require attaching markers or QR codes to equipment and materials to align positions, this approach cross-references the shape of the equipment and materials captured by the tablet camera with the 3D design, enabling use even indoors where securing satellite signals is difficult. Through this, inspectors first check for major quality issues such as missing components, incorrect installation, and abnormal positions or orientations, and then conduct a detailed inspection by using a 3D laser scanner to precisely measure the actual shape and compare it with design criteria for parts that require additional verification. GS Engineering & Construction expects that by sequentially using AR-based inspections and 3D laser scanning, it can reduce the time required for quality inspections and improve the accuracy and efficiency of inspections by focusing resources on items that require detailed checks. GS Engineering & Construction has applied quality inspections using Augmented Reality (AR) technology at four ongoing plant sites in and outside Korea. Based on the technology and operational experience accumulated in this process, it plans to expand application to areas that require factory fabrication and repetitive quality inspections, such as steel modular. It also plans to systematically accumulate and manage inspection results and quality history data going forward to continuously advance the digitalization of the quality inspection process.

title: GS Caltex Coach's 14-Loss Turnaround to Championship - 조선일보
content: Lee Young-Taek Vows to Embrace 'All-In' Strategy Despite Controversy [Sports Chosun Kim Young-rok Reporter] "After 14 consecutive losses, I said, 'I should quit...'" Turning criticism into praise, transforming hardship into joy. It was a two-year journey between heaven and hell. Lee Young-Taek, the GS Caltex head coach, is the protagonist. Lee Young-Taek said, "Every moment of the spring volleyball season is still vivid in my memory. However, the afterglow of the championship doesn’t linger much. It really felt like it ended the moment I woke up the next day." It was a dramatic turnaround for the coach who stood on the edge of the cliff just a year ago. Lee Young-Taek identified the most critical hurdle as the semi-playoffs against Heungkuk Life. "It was a match with a tremendous amount of pressure. During the championship series, winning the first game in Gimcheon was important, but securing the second game was decisive." In the 2024–2025 season, shortly after his appointment, GS Caltex struggled with 14 consecutive losses. However, in the 2025–2026 season, they achieved a historic comeback, rising as champions. After advancing to the postseason as the third-place team in the regular league, they defeated Heungkuk Life, Hyundai Engineering & Construction, and Korea Expressway Corporation in six consecutive matches, completing an "upset victory" that will go down in history. Lee Young-Taek even expressed his intention to resign during the 14 consecutive losses. However, Kim Yong-Hee, the GS Caltex team president, and Kim Sun-Wook, the general manager, strongly persuaded him to stay. Choi Tae-Woong, a former Hyundai Capital head coach and one year Lee’s senior at Hanyang University, also visited the training facility to support him. As a result, they achieved a second-half turnaround and escaped the cellar. Last season was even more dramatic. GS Caltex fell to fifth place after the fourth round but surged to third in the regular league with four consecutive wins at the end. They then went on to win the championship. Reflecting on the postseason, Lee Young-Taek said, "We adjusted our substitutions and tactical timing faster than usual, which worked well." However, he promised to return to being a "patient coach" in the new season. He emphasized, "To develop players, you have to give them consistent opportunities." Regarding the so-called "all-in" controversy, he stated he would not avoid the issue. He also recalled Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance, which repeatedly frustrated him during his playing days. "I won the regular league but never the championship finals. From 2011 to 2013, I lost three consecutive championship finals. Back then, Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance’s ‘all-in’ strategy was unstoppable even when we knew it. Having such a foreign player is a blessing, and a setter’s ability to consistently deliver the ball is crucial. The sacrifice of players who handle reception and defense is also necessary." Before the postseason, Lee Young-Taek gave his setters the game records from Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance’s matches. GS Caltex has Silva, who is no less formidable than Gavin and Leo from that era. He explained, "Gavin had a 70% attack share and a 70% success rate. Since every postseason match is a single game, I told our setters not to hesitate and to serve the ball freely." "When you win the championship, everyone contributes to the success. Silva received the MVP, but ultimately, all the players remained as champions." Preparing for the new season as a "championship-winning coach" brings more pressure. He expressed regret, saying, "After winning, my standards have risen, so there are many aspects I’m not satisfied with," while highlighting setters Kim Ji-Won and Park Sa-Rang as key players. To reduce the burden on Silva, the "problem solver" who has surpassed 1,000 points for three consecutive years, diversifying attacks is necessary. The same expectation applies to the newly joined Asian Quota player Tanacha. However, he has no intention of avoiding his team’s strongest weapon. "Serving strong spikes and finishing with blocks is the most ideal volleyball. While distributing attacks evenly is good, it’s not as easy as it sounds. Maximizing Silva’s abilities is also our team’s strength. We won’t hesitate when it’s time to take risks."

The unidentified man was the only juror who voted to convict Clancy and refused to change his verdict, resulting in a hung jury. The GiveSendGo, titled Stand With the Juror, has raised more than $126,000 US for the man in case he faces any professional fallout over his role in the mistrial. "One juror held his seat. He looked at what she did, not the brand of Zoloft. So the defense demanded the judge throw him off the jury for 'not following reasonable doubt,' " the fundraiser, started by Tom Hennessey, reads. "The judge left him on. The jury hung. Mistrial. Now she can be tried again for killing her children instead of getting a standing ovation for her symptoms," the message continues. "We're not letting this slide. If they come for him, and they will, this is to cover security, lawyers, and lost work." WBTS reported that the holdout, believed to be a man in his 30s, was charged in 2021 with assaulting his then-wife, though the charge was later dismissed. The man's nephew, who was 13 at the time, reportedly called police after alleging that he saw his uncle grab her by the throat and throw her into a dresser, according to the outlet. They divorced after the charges were dismissed, with the outlet reporting that his ex-wife did not want to testify in the case out of fear of losing custody of her daughter. The nephew, however, still has has an active restraining order against his uncle, which references the 2021 incident. An affidavit filed by the nephew alleged that the juror pushed him to the ground and repeatedly punched him in the face. Florida Gov. content:
To the extent that historical press releases reference BMW Manufacturing Co., LLC as the manufacturer of certain X model vehicles, the referenced vehicles are manufactured in South Carolina with a combination of U.S. origin and imported parts and components. Oleg SatanovskyBMW Group
