. The tenth BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy got
  underway yesterday. Camped on the edge of the village of Coltesti,
  overlooked by a 13th century clifftop fortress, deep in the
  Transylvanian region, the competitors are surrounded by a natural
  wilderness landscape. Encircled by the Carpathian mountains and some
  of Europe’s few great undisturbed natural forests – home to apex
  predators such as grey wolves and brown bears, in their thousands –
  this is a rare European wilderness. Rugged terrain in the form of dense forests, gravel roads, river
  crossings, and mountainous ascents and descents will challenge the
  riders in the coming days. A perfect tableau on which to showcase the
  impressive on- and off-road capabilities of the latest GS Trophy
  Competition Bike, the BMW R 12 G/S. The BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy is emphatically not a race:
  outright speed, fastest times and individual victory are not what
  define success. Instead, it is a shared adventure that rewards precise
  riding, sound judgement, endurance and, above all, the ability to work
  as a team. Participants support one another, solve practical and
  intellectual challenges together and demonstrate the camaraderie,
  resilience and mutual respect at the heart of the international GS
  community. While teams collect points during special tests, these
  challenges are designed to showcase well-rounded adventure-riding
  skills rather than racing performance.
Over the weekend, participants completed registration and medical
  checks, as well as the individual fitting of their protective and
  riding equipment. After the SENA communication systems had been
  integrated, they took delivery of their personalised BMW R 12 G/S
  motorcycles. A welcome dinner and team introductions on Saturday set
  the stage for the start on Sunday morning.
This year, eight national or regional qualifiers have produced 13
  international teams, eight of which are three-person male teams and
  five two-person female teams – all together 30 riders from 13 nations.
  Some 30 individuals who will need all their riding skills, their inner
  strength and outgoing team working capability to succeed in this
  ever-testing adventure motorcycling competition.
Martin Schleypen, Event Director and Head of Brand Management,
  BMW Motorrad, speaking from base camp:
“The GS Trophy brings together people from all around the world
  who share a common passion: adventure, adventure riding, and the BMW
  GS. It is far more than a competition. It is about team spirit,
  international friendships, and shared experiences that continue to
  resonate long after the event has ended.For me, this unique sense
  of community is what truly defines the magic of the GS Trophy.”

Adventure riding without limits. The participants face six days and around 1,500 challenging
  kilometres through the Carpathians. Roughly half of the route runs off
  paved roads, taking in steep sections, rugged mountain trails and
  dense forest tracks. The winding asphalt roads also demand maximum
  concentration due to the challenging topography. Daily competition challenges test riding, practical and mental skills
  – essential qualities for adventure riders operating in remote regions. The tenth edition is held under the motto “Back to Basics”: demanding
  rides through mountain and forest terrain, teamwork and the certainty
  that the unexpected is always just around the corner. Host country Romania captivates with its rich traditions, fascinating
  history and warm hospitality – a far more authentic experience than
  the fantasy imagery shaped by Bram Stoker’s Dracula. It’s time to meet the GS riders. Below is a full list of the teams,

title: "Watching a Japanese off-season overseas training session!" GS Caltex continues its "special journey" with fans for the third year... Yoo Seo-yeon: "I feel an even greater sense of responsibility" - starnewskorea.com

The unique fan culture of GS Caltex, where fans accompany the team at off-season training camps to pray for success in the new season, continues for the third consecutive year. GS Caltex announced that it conducted an 'Overseas Training Camp Fan Tour' from the 12th to the 14th, a two-night, three-day trip in Mito and Hitachinaka cities, Japan. This tour included 15 accompanying fans. According to the club, participants visited the training ground of sister team Astemo Rivale in Hitachinaka on the afternoon of the 13th to watch a practice match. title: St. G's Bodega Opens Wednesday On East St. Germain - WJON
content: If you’ve ever wished you could run into a neighborhood store for a few groceries without having to walk through an entire supermarket, St. Cloud’s East End has something new for you. St. G’s Bodega is opening this week, just in time for the third annual Festi-Fall! Something exciting is happening again on the East End of St. Cloud, and this time it comes with sandwiches, snacks, groceries, and a little bit of neighborhood convenience. St. G’s Bodega is opening its doors Wednesday, September 16th, at 11 a.m. at 415 E. St. Germain Street, right next door to The Kitchenette and Sage & Salvage. The timing couldn't be better, because the third annual Festi-Fall is also happening on the East End this week. Now, if you are like me, you might hear the word “bodega” and wonder exactly what that means. A 'bodega' is essentially a small neighborhood grocery or convenience store. The word is especially common in places like New York City and in Latino communities, where bodegas have long been a part of everyday neighborhood life. Bodegas are the kind of place where you can run in for a few things without walking through a giant grocery store just to get bread, milk, or whatever else you forgot. St. G's Bodega is being created to serve the neighborhood and make those quick trips a whole lot easier. Instead of getting in the car and heading to a large-format grocery store for just a couple of essentials, you can stop at St. G’s and grab what you need. This is the kind of store I've been missing for years. I'm close enough that I can stop by and check it out! The store will carry essential groceries, personal care items, household products, and tobacco products. St. G’s Bodega will also have tables near the front window where customers can sit down for a sandwich and a drink. I love the idea of that because it gives the place a little more of a neighborhood feel. It sounds like somewhere you can stop in, grab a bite, take a few minutes, and actually enjoy the space and maybe even meet a few of your neighbors. The business is owned by the Waseka women, Marla, Madison, and Shaelynn. I've stayed in touch with them over the past few years, and they are clear on their goals: to create a welcoming neighborhood environment that is convenient for the people who live and work nearby, while also giving visitors another reason to spend some time on the East End. “St. G” refers to Saint Germain, who the owners describe as a very diverse and interesting character. It is a name that seems to fit the personality they want for the business, too. The opening is another addition to an East End of St. Cloud that has continued to see small businesses and community activity bring more people to the area. With Festi-Fall taking place this week, there should be plenty of people checking out what is happening around the neighborhood, and now they will have a new place to discover. title: Friends remember Springfield bartender for her joy, rally around injured coworker - ky3.com
content: SPRINGFIELD, Mo. (KY3) - Friends and coworkers gathered at Mama G’s Kitchen in downtown Springfield to remember Tesia Ta, who died after a car crash on Sept. 2, and to support coworker Kayle Moore, who was seriously injured in the crash. Police said Moore was turning her SUV into a business on E. Kearney St. when it was hit by a Mercedes. Investigators suspect speeding and impairment by the driver of the Mercedes. The investigation remains open. Ta, who was riding with Moore, later died. She was 34. Moore is now home after two surgeries. Mama G’s Kitchen owner Gloria Hairston said Moore will be unable to work for a while. Ta worked as a bartender at Mama G’s Kitchen, where she also taught twerk classes. “Tesia was my bartender. And I would say, my second daughter,” said Hairston. “Because all my employees I just bring in, and I’m their mama. So, yes, we got really close with her working here.” Bar lead Hawk Johnson, Ta’s friend and coworker, said Ta faced stage-four kidney failure and underwent weekly dialysis. “She had a superpower, I would say. So they say, like, people are a beam of sunlight. Tesia was a spotlight,” Johnson said. Johnson said that after watching dialysis wear Ta down, Johnson offered to donate a kidney to her. Johnson said three days of testing in Kansas City showed the two were compatible, and the transplant was about a month away when Ta died. Johnson said their last conversation was about the life Ta planned after the transplant. Johnson had already prepared a bedroom for her. “I had actually converted one of my bedrooms into a room for her that I never got the chance to offer for her to live with me. I don’t know when I’m going to take it down, but it won’t be for a while,” Johnson said. Mama G’s Kitchen is donating 20% of the day’s sales, along with direct donations collected during the event. title: Donghae launches AI committee to build industrial ecosystem around GS data center - The Herald Business - 헤럴드경제
content: Donghae, a city in Gangwon Province where GS Group plans to build an AI data center, is establishing an artificial intelligence committee to chart the industrial development path the facility is expected to open up. The city will launch the Donghae AI Committee and hold its inaugural meeting on Wednesday. The committee will discuss in concrete terms the AI policies and projects the city needs to pursue, including development strategies that link the data center to local industries. The 21-member body will draw on experts from the public sector, military, industry, academia and research institutions. It will advise on and propose policy across five areas: drawing up an AI industry development plan, advancing AI transformation in civil society, reviewing major AI-related policies and initiatives, responding to government AI grant programs and pending projects, and devising strategies to leverage the data center for broader regional development. The move signals the city's ambition to go beyond simply landing the data center — whose construction investment alone is expected to reach around 100 trillion won ($74.3 billion) — and instead build a comprehensive corporate city that integrates an AI-linked industrial ecosystem with culture and tourism. The committee plans to work through the post-attraction challenges step by step: identifying which industries and companies to bring in, determining how to cultivate local talent and create jobs, and mapping out how the city and its residents will make the transition to AI-driven administration and daily life. Alongside this, the city plans to explore ways to merge AI technology with Donghae's core local industries — including logistics and energy — and to proactively pursue new projects tied to national AI policy, laying the groundwork for what officials are calling a "Donghae-style AI ecosystem." The inaugural meeting will focus on sharing the city's AI project roadmap and the current status of the data center development, with priority discussion on what steps must be taken first to translate the data center into tangible local growth — connecting it to regional industries, talent development and job creation. "Securing the AI data center is just the starting point," said Lee Seon-u, Donghae's director of planning and budget. "What matters is how we connect it to real growth for the city — in industry, jobs and talent development. Through the AI committee, we will gather expert opinion from all sectors and work through, one by one, the tasks Donghae needs to start preparing for right now."

title: Lee Young-taek Balances 'All-In' Strategy With Offensive Diversification - 조선일보
content: Championship-winning coach leverages Silva's strength while integrating Japanese staff to expand attack options “The joy of winning? I woke up and it was already over.” For Lee Young-taek, 49, the head coach of GS Caltex in the women’s professional volleyball league, the past two seasons have been a rollercoaster. After a 14-game losing streak in the 2024–2025 season that made him consider resigning, he led his team to a historic upset victory in the 2025–2026 spring season, earning the title of “championship-winning coach.” Under his guidance, GS Caltex entered the postseason as the third seed and defeated the fourth-seeded Heungkuk Life in a single-round playoff, the second-seeded Hyundai Engineering & Construction in a best-of-three series, and the first-seeded Korea Expressway Corporation in a best-of-five championship series, winning six consecutive games to complete a perfect “upset victory.” However, the joy of reaching the summit was short-lived. “I still vividly remember every moment of the spring season games. But the afterglow of the championship doesn’t linger much. It really felt like it ended the moment I woke up the next day.” On the 13th, at the team’s training camp in Hitachinaka, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan, Lee identified the semifinal playoff as the most critical turning point in the previous season’s championship run. “Advancing past the semifinal was the biggest factor. It was a high-pressure match. In the finals, winning the first game in Gimcheon was important, but securing the second game was even more crucial.” ◇ “During the 14-game losing streak, I thought about quitting” Now a championship-winning coach, Lee stood on the brink of the cliff during the 2024–2025 season. GS Caltex fell into a historic 14-game losing streak in the first half. Reflecting on that period, Lee admitted, “I even considered resigning.” Despite setbacks like player injuries, he blamed himself rather than making excuses. “I felt it was my lack of ability that led to the losing streak. I even told the club I wanted to step down.” However, Kim Yong-hee, the team’s general manager, and Kim Sun-wook, the office director, persuaded him to stay. Choi Tae-woong, a former Hyundai Capital coach and a year senior from Hanyang University, also visited the training facility to support Lee. GS Caltex rallied in the second half to avoid last place. Last season, the team struggled to a fifth-place finish after four rounds but climbed to third with a late four-game winning streak, culminating in a miraculous championship. Through this journey, Lee himself evolved. While he patiently nurtured young players during the regular season, he shifted to a more aggressive approach in the playoffs. “The postseason is a short, single-elimination battle. I decided to make quicker substitutions and tactical decisions compared to the regular season. That strategy worked well.” He added that he would return to his patient coaching style during the upcoming regular season. “To develop players, you have to keep giving them opportunities. Fans might say, ‘The coach is passive’ or ‘He’s just standing by,’ but I’m not doing it without purpose. Haha.” Lee is often labeled as a coach who employs an “all-in” strategy, concentrating attacks on a single player. While this term is typically used negatively, Lee disagrees. “I don’t view ‘all-in’ negatively. It’s also a form of ability.” Lee has a painful memory from his playing days. As a player for Korean Air, he faced Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance in the championship series and repeatedly lost to their dominant foreign attackers, Gavin and Leo. “As a player, I won the regular season but never the championship. I fell victim to Samsung’s ‘all-in’ strategy. I knew it was coming but couldn’t stop it. From 2011 to 2013, I lost three consecutive championship series. But even that, I consider their strength. Having the resources to recruit such foreign players is luck, and the setter’s ability to consistently deliver the ball to them is skill. It also requires the sacrifice of players in reception and defense.” This experience became a vital lesson when Lee became a coach. Before the postseason last season, he retrieved Samsung’s game records from his playing days and handed them to his setters. “Back then, Gavin had a 70% attack share with a 70% success rate. We lost, and Samsung won the championship. That record remains eternal.” He then told his setters, “This is a single-elimination battle, so don’t hold back. Don’t hesitate—give Silva the ball freely.” In the semifinal, Silva’s attack share soared to nearly 50%, with a 50% success rate. Far from satisfied, Lee jokingly “criticized” the setters before the next game. “You did well, but I don’t think you fed Silva as much as I expected. A 50% success rate in women’s volleyball is incredible, but I said, ‘You can feed her even more.’ I didn’t want the players to be conscious of the phrase, ‘Silva is carrying the team alone.’ If we win, everyone is a champion.” GS Caltex eventually claimed the title, and Silva was named MVP. Lee emphasized, “Silva received the MVP, but all the players remain as champions.” ◇ “This year’s pressure is incomparable to last year’s” Winning once doesn’t ease the mind—it heightens expectations. Lee admitted, “The pressure and worries I feel now are incomparable to what I felt starting last season.” “Maybe my standards have risen after winning. The players performed so well last spring. But seeing how they’re preparing now, there are still aspects I’m not satisfied with, and some weaknesses remain. That worries me.” For the new season, Lee revamped the coaching staff by hiring two Japanese coaches. He explained that the players wanted to learn Japan’s technical and training methods. “Our domestic coaches are skilled and dedicated, but there’s a trend among players wanting to learn from Japanese coaches. Considering their requests, we hired them, and the satisfaction is high.” Kawamura Shinji, an outside hitter turned coach, previously led a men’s team in Japan’s V-League. Kwon Min-ji, a key player in last season’s championship, frequently consults him. The other Japanese coach, Ishii Suguru, specializes in setters. With Ahn Hye-jin’s departure, the team’s success hinges on how well Kim Ji-won and new recruit Park Sa-rang fill the gap. Lee said, “Kim Ji-won and Park Sa-rang could be the key players this season.” The team’s focus for the new season is diversifying their offense. While Silva remains a reliable scorer, Lee wants to reduce her burden. Silva became the first V-League player to score over 1,000 points in three consecutive seasons. In this context, the new Asian Quota player, Thanacha from Thailand, is a key addition. “If Thanacha’s attacks flow smoothly, the setters will have more options. Improved efficiency from middle blockers can also lessen Silva’s load.” However, Lee has no intention of hiding his team’s strongest weapon. “My ideal volleyball involves powerful serves and decisive blocks. Distributing attacks evenly is good, but it’s not easy. We have Silva, an exceptional foreign player. Maximizing her abilities is our strength. We should leverage our strengths and address weaknesses.” Silva had the most attack attempts in the V-League last season but also the highest success rate at 47.33%. This season, Lee must prove that last year’s victory was not a fluke. His answer from last spring’s tournament is simple: “We’ll maximize our strengths and not hesitate when it’s time to fight.”

title: Vikings vs. Packers Game Observations: Classic Look in Epic Comeback - Minnesota Vikings
content:
MINNEAPOLIS — The Vikings uniforms were the Classic style. The team's fourth quarter was epic. Minnesota opened its 2026 regular season by outlasting Green Bay for a 39-22 victory Sunday at U.S. Bank Stadium. The victory involved emerging from a double-digit deficit (22-10 with 5:09 remaining in the third quarter) by scoring 29 unanswered points, a run that began with a 16-yard touchdown pass from T.J. Hockenson that was precipitated by a career-long 68-yard kickoff return by second-year pro Myles Price. That score made it 22-17 with 3:01 left in the third quarter. Green Bay tried to answer, but instead of taking three points on a field goal, Packers Head Coach Matt LaFleur accepted an offsides penalty and opted to go for it on fourth-and-1. QB Jordan Love was stuffed by a wall of Purple led by rookie Domonique Orange, providing a major turning point. View game action photos from the Vikings Week 1 game vs. the Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium. Minnesota drove 83 yards on its next possession, ticking off more than six minutes before Aaron Jones, Sr., scored on a 3-yard romp to the left pylon. He picked up key blocks from Christian Darrisaw and rookie fullback Max Bredeson. A 2-point conversion pass from Wentz to Justin Jefferson made it 25-22 with 6:37 remaining. Playing defense ramped up the pressure, forcing turnovers when Andrew Van Ginkel forced a fumble during a sack of Love that was split with Blake Cashman. Van Ginkel returned the ball to the 1, and Jordan Mason followed with a TD plunge. Cashman tipped a pass by Love, and it deflected off Harrison Smith before it was corralled by James Pierre and returned to set up another short field. Jefferson capped the next drive with a 9-yard touchdown on his 587th career reception, which tied Randy Moss for second on the team's receptions leaderboard. The long-awaited start to the 2026 Vikings season began auspiciously. Minnesota's offense lost a yard on its first run play and the football on its first pass play. After Aaron Jones, Sr., was tackled for a loss of 1, quarterback Kyler Murray launched a pass into double coverage toward fellow newcomer Jauan Jennings. It was intercepted by Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon and returned 11 yards to the Green Bay 47. The Packers only gained 12 yards on the ensuing possession but it was enough for rookie Trey Smack to drill a 59-yard field goal with room to spare for a 3-0 lead with 12:11 remaining in the first quarter. Murray's second possession included a 6-yard run by Jones, a 9-yard pass to Justin Jefferson and a 6-yard scramble by Murray before back-to-back false starts by Minnesota halted the momentum. On the next series, three plays after an 81-yard touchdown allowed by the Vikings, Murray scrambled again. He gave himself up by sliding shy of the sticks, but was hit in the helmet by Lukas Van Ness and smacked by Javon Bullard on the turf. Officials flagged Bullard for unnecessary roughness. Murray was evaluated for a concussion and ruled out. He finished his Vikings debut was replaced by Wentz, who finished 12-of-19 passing for 133 yards and three touchdowns, good for a passer rating of 123.5. Wentz showed his veteran savvy to strike for Minnesota's first touchdown of the season. He alertly used a hard count to draw Van Ness offsides and opted to take an end zone shot to Jefferson, who was in single coverage by rookie corner Brandon Cisse. Jefferson reeled in the catch to make it a 12-10 contest with 1:55 remaining in the first half. It was a free play similar to many that Green Bay has capitalized on over the years. The 39-yard distance was a longer TD pass than Minnesota posted in the entire 2025 season, by the way. The Vikings stayed patient with the run game and eventually wore down the Packers. Mason led the way with 59 yards on 15 carries, and Jones finished with 40 yards on 12 carries. The persistence helped Minnesota win time of possession 32:58 to 27:02 and took away a few opportunities for a Packers offense that put together some explosives, including an 81-yard touchdown from Love to Christian Watson. The defense also showed relentlessness and finally found a way home, despite Love's elusiveness and ability to throw on the run. Van Ginkel led Minnesota with 1.5 sacks, and Cashman had the other half. Levi Drake Rodriguez and Dallas Turner each recorded one. Turner recorded a whopping seven of Minnesota's 15 QB hits. Orange's play on the QB sneak was massive and joined by other times he was pushing the line of scrimmage. Pierre's pick was the fifth of his career and a great way to make his Minnesota debut after 95 career games with the Steelers. DeeJay Dallas signed to Minnesota's practice squad on Sept. 2. He was elevated Saturday. Known as an all-around running back with rush, receiving and return yards, he showed he can also lay the hammer. Dallas' block sprung Price's long return. Bredeson showed full bandwidth in the offense, moving to multiple spots in the formation and delivering key blocks. title: Hana Securities lifts GS E&C target on Korea Donghae AI data center bets - CHOSUNBIZ - Chosunbiz
content: Hana Securities on the 14th raised its target price for GS Engineering & Construction(36,850 won ▼ 950 -2.51%), reflecting expectations of orders for the Donghae data center. It kept its "Buy" rating and lifted the target price to 40,000 won from 36,000 won. GS Engineering & Construction's previous day's closing price was 38,500 won. Kim Seung-jun, an analyst at Hana Securities, said, "The Donghae data center is proceeding as planned, so we reflected fourth-quarter order expectations in the valuation upgrade," adding, "There are five data centers to be carried out from last year to this year, and through the Donghae project we can expect orders for data centers on a gigawatt scale." He added, "Because orders exceeding 10 trillion won can contribute to revenue within two to three years, the pace of companywide revenue growth could be very fast." GS Group said when it announced its three mega projects that it would complete an artificial intelligence (AI) data center totaling 2.4 GW in Bukpyeong Second Industrial Complex in Donghae by 2028 for 1.2 GW (phase one) and by 2029 for 1.2 GW (phase two). GS Engineering & Construction established the GSAI Infrastructure entity to develop the data center and set up subsidiaries including Donghae AI Campus 1, Donghae AI Campus 2, and Donghae AI Campus 3. Kim said, "A plan is reportedly under review to expand in stages, starting with groundbreaking for 100 MW and adding further capacity," adding, "The land-use change has been completed, and the final review of the power system impact assessment has also passed." The remaining step now is the building permit. It is reported that the application was filed in early last month and is under review. The building permit application covers only the phase-one project of 1.2 GW to be developed by 2028. After approval is granted in September or October, the project is estimated to be on track with a target to break ground in November. Kim said, "If the scale is 100 MW, the order value is estimated at 1 trillion won, and it can contribute to GS Engineering & Construction's consolidation results." On top of that, there is an outlook that results will improve starting in the second half. In the second quarter, about 50 billion won in expected losses were booked in plants (incinerator operations), and roughly 100 billion won including bad debt write-offs in SG&A were reflected, leading to weak results for GS Engineering & Construction. From the second half, these one-off expenses are excluded, leaving room for an improvement in results. Analysts say margins can be expected in building and housing. title: These 5 Adventure Motorcycles Are The Only Bikes Your Garage Really Needs - HotCars
content: Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update The adventure bike market has evolved into a truly diverse space. It is fair to say that there is an ADV out there for pretty much anyone, no matter your shape, size, or riding preference. These dual-purpose motorcycles are more popular than ever these days, largely thanks to how versatile they are. Within this segment, it is the middleweight bikes that really stand out as the most versatile. Light enough to be effective off-road and comfortable enough to spend the day on the highway if necessary, these bikes offer us a means to own just one motorcycle that can do pretty much everything. Well, almost everything, we don’t exactly recommend taking one of these bikes to a track day! It took Ducati some time before they released a dedicated adventure bike, but the DesertX was well worth the wait. The latest model gets revised styling, and an all-new powertrain. The one thing we certainly didn’t want to see change too much was the styling, which made it one of the most attractive adventure bikes on the market. Mercifully, it is more a case of evolution than revolution in that respect. It still looks fantastic. Underneath the gorgeous outer shell lies the new desmo-less 890cc V2 engine. It caused a bit of a stir when it made its debut on the Panigale, because it has so much less power than the outgoing model. Here with the DesertX there is no such concern because the power figures are more or less unchanged, with the bike making 110 horsepower and 68 pound feet of torque. BMW did a great job of getting the latest F 900 GS right in line with the competition in terms of performance and weight. One minor frustration, which has absolutely nothing to do with the quality of the motorcycle itself, is how BMW structures the pricing. On paper, this actually looks like a great deal. BMW is a premium brand, after all, and at this price it undercuts several competitors. Unfortunately, this is nowhere near the actual out-the-door price. Several nice-to-have features are left optional, and if you are not careful, simply checking options boxes will see the price soar past the aforementioned Ducati. Which, incidentally, has pretty much everything already you might want fitted as standard. Even the color you see in these pictures is optional. But, as long as you come into the purchase fully aware of this, and certain of which options you want, and which you can live without, it is still well worth considering. The Tuareg Rally 660 neatly splits the difference between the more affordable Japanese bikes, and the two premium European options above. While significantly more expensive than the base model Tuareg, we feel the upgrades are all things enthusiasts would consider turning to the aftermarket for anyway, and the total cost would most likely eventually add up to more than the additional $1,500 you need to fork out for the Rally spec. The SC Project exhaust alone would likely set you back close to $1,000 if you were to turn to the aftermarket. While it doesn’t increase horsepower, it shaves 12 pounds off of what is already a very light middleweight. That is more weight than most of us would lose, even on the strictest of diets. It also gets a high-mount fender (which tends to split opinion, but we like it), a more robust skid plate, Ergal rims, and a unique Rally livery. Ever since the Tenere 700 first came out, enthusiasts have been going on about what it could be with the addition of this or that. The World Raid version puts all of those theories to bed once and for all. It is absolutely everything you need rolled into one exceptional adventure bike, and the added $2,000 over and above what you would be spending on the base model seems like a pretty good deal from where we are standing. The base model was always pretty handy off-road, but the fully adjustable KYB suspension (as well as a steering stabilizer) you get here most certainly takes it to the next level. It also gets a sophisticated IMU-enhanced electronics suite, so lean sensitive traction control and cornering ABS are present. A long-range tank and a redesigned skid plate round out what is a comprehensive package. It is most certainly heavier than the base model, but much of that added weight comes in the form of fuel. Don’t let its purposeful off-road design fool you. Although it is a capable off-road ADV, the Transalp’s key strength is actually how comfortable it is. Out of all the bikes on this list, it might actually be the most comfortable tourer, but with a wet weight of just 468 pounds, it is still relatively light. So while touring might be its key point of difference, it will also handle the daily commute with ease. Its ability to be used as a weekday commuter has also been enhanced with the addition of an E-Clutch for a mere $200 more than last year’s model. What makes Honda’s E-Clutch so innovative is the fact that it offers riders the best of both worlds kind of solution. It acts like a twist-and-go automatic when you want, which adds a layer of convenience in town, or on long, boring stretches of highway, and it works like any manual when you want that, like when you are riding off-road. It even acts like a quickshifter on more spirited rides. Along with the E-Clutch, Honda also finally caved and gave the bike a skid plate, something the original version didn't have, which was a bit odd for any form of ADV, even if it is a little more street oriented. They also gave the bike fully adjustable suspension, which was not a glaring omission at all, and most certainly counts as a nice-to-have feature for a bike this affordable. We want to hear from you. title: "A GS with an LS:" Classic 1970 Buick Skylark Won't Make You Feel Blue About Its Few Modern Touches - autoevolution
content:
The Buick Skylark nameplate was made across six generations over the span of almost half a century, from 1953 through 1998, and remains an example of how the automotive realm has been dramatically reshaped over the years via advancing technology, changing buyer taste, and new standards. The A-body third generation was offered as a four-door hardtop or sedan and station wagon, as well as a two-door coupe, convertible, and hardtop. It was noted for its muscle car/personal luxury car appeal, and it shared components with the likes of the Acadian Beaumont, Buick Special, Chevrolet Chevelle, Pontiac Tempest and LeMans plus GTO, Oldsmobile F-85, Cutlass and Cutlass Supreme, or the Hurst/Olds and Buick GSX and Chevelle SS for the performance models. This 1970 Buick Skylark GS “is a striking example of classic Buick muscle reimagined with modern performance and drivability,” according to the dealership’s description. It went through a frame-off restoration combined with a few sensible modifications, and now this Skylark “combines the aggressive proportions and unmistakable styling of a first-generation GS with a thoroughly modernized mechanical package.” Outside, it’s dressed in a serene combination of Stratomist Blue and chrome trimmings, while inside there’s a classic black interior to show that despite the beautiful shade, nobody should feel blue about its classic car potential. There are also numerous chrome accents, larger Ridler aftermarket wheels, and a contemporary heart. That’s because under the hood resides a 5.3-liter LS V8 paired to a 4L60E automatic transmission, offering modern performance and reliability to the classic Buick. Plus, there’s power steering and air conditioning to “further enhance the driving experience, making this Skylark far more comfortable and usable than a typical vintage muscle car.” The chassis has also been updated to match the powertrain: it features a coilover suspension setup, front power disc brakes, and a few other modern touches. However, once you’re inside, the vintage atmosphere is still present and accounted for. The company says that you’ll have “a unique muscle car that grabs attention at the cruise-in while holding the road on the cruise out.” But how much does it cost? Well, the aftermarket dealership asks exactly $67,900, which is less than the starting price of a 2027 C8 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray, for example. Maybe that’s not a good comparison, but sadly that’s the only remaining passenger car line sold by General Motors in the mainstream sector, along with Cadillac’s outgoing CT4 and the surviving CT5 luxury sedans. So, what do you think – would you buy this 1970 Buick Skylark GS featuring an LS or not? title: Kim Ji-won Seeks Redemption, Second Title with Tana Char - 조선일보
content: GS Caltex setter targets consecutive championships after regrets from limited spring play [Sports Chosun Kim Young-rok Reporter] "I’ve won two championships, but I still have some regrets about not being able to play many games in the spring volleyball season. I want to show a different side this year." The joy of the championship setter was short-lived, as the women’s volleyball offseason is brief. GS Caltex’s Kim Ji-won is burning with determination to win the new season. GS Caltex continues its fourth year alongside the 'Cuban monster' Giselle Silva. However, Silva, born in 1991, will turn 36 years old next year. She herself has said, "This is the twilight of my playing career. I want to retire while I can still show my skills to the fans." Naturally, GS Caltex’s focus is on the present rather than the future. The core player who must lead the team 'now' is Kim Ji-won. Regarding her post-championship vacation, Kim Ji-won said, "There was nothing special. However, I was surprised to find I had gained weight after taking a long break from exercise. Now, my body feels lighter again," and laughed. She is gradually returning to practice matches in preparation for the season opener. "In my first year, our team achieved a treble (winning the cup tournament, regular season, and championship finals all in a single season). I couldn’t do anything due to injuries that season. Last season was different. Since I directly contributed to the matches, even after winning the championship, I couldn’t believe it. I don’t know how many times I rewatched the championship match footage during the offseason." It was a season where her skills truly flourished. She played 35 games and 109 sets, exceeding 1,200 sets with a 1200-set accuracy. Her average of 11.03 sets per game is her best record since her debut. Kim Ji-won reflected, "Since the team’s performance wasn’t great, I struggled mentally during preparation. As the season progressed, our momentum improved, and the good results made me very happy." Previously, GS Caltex, which had failed to advance to the spring volleyball season despite two seasons with league-best foreign player Silva, barely made it to the spring volleyball after a fierce battle until the final game of last season, Silva’s third year in Korea. Once there, everything changed. They dominated the court with a perfect 6-0 record against Jungwon Life Insurance, Hyundai Engineering & Construction, and Korea Expressway Corporation, clinching their first championship in five years. However, there was a slight regret in the process. The regular season was operated primarily around Kim Ji-won, but as the season ended, the role of An Hye-jin (free agent), who returned from injury, grew larger. Ultimately, An Hye-jin was the starting setter in the spring volleyball. Kim Ji-won said, "It wasn’t just me who led the team to the spring volleyball," but added, "There’s still some regret. We won the championship, but I didn’t get to play much." She continued, "Still, if it’s the way the team can win, I think I was still lacking." The biggest wall in her career has been Hyundai Engineering & Construction. GS Caltex has struggled every year against Hyundai Engineering & Construction’s high blocks due to their weak middle blockers. Kim Ji-won sensed victory after winning the first playoff game against Hyundai Engineering & Construction. This season, she also named Hyundai Engineering & Construction as the most burdensome team. Although Yang Hyo-jin and Lee Da-hyun have left, the team remains formidable with Kim Da-in still present, joined by Bae Yu-na and Mega. Kim Ji-won was selected as the first overall pick in the rookie draft and joined GS Caltex. At the time, many volleyball insiders questioned the choice of Kim Ji-won over Lee Sun-woo (Jung Kwan Jang) and Choi Jung-min (Industrial Bank of Korea (IBK)). However, GS Caltex proved that their first picks, from Han Soo-jin to Kim Ji-won, were not surprises. Kim Ji-won laughed, "As a rookie, I felt pressured. It was unexpected, and there were so many negative comments. Now, I feel more at ease." GS Caltex’s clubhouse is located in the mountains of Cheongpyeong. Kim Ji-won said, "In summer, there are so many bugs that we can’t open the windows. In winter, when it snows a lot, cars slip on the uphill roads. That’s why I bought a four-wheel-drive car. During peak summer season, the roads get completely clogged," but added, "We have to drive to the convenience store. The facilities are amazing. It’s truly the best place to focus on training," and laughed. This year, GS Caltex strengthened its wing line by adding Tana Char as an Asian quota player, joining Silva. Tana Char’s transfer comes from the team they faced in last season’s championship finals. The chemistry between Kim Ji-won and Tana Char could be a key factor in this season’s performance. "When she was on the opposite side of the net, Silva and Tana Char felt similar—roaring and overwhelming. Now that we’re on the same team, I realized they’re more four-dimensional than I thought. It’s hard to explain. Even though Silva is my senior, she has a cute side. With Silva and Tana Char, my role will definitely expand. This year, I want to show more diverse aspects. I want to become a setter like Han Seon-su (Hanwha Aerospace) who maintains strong mental resilience and leads the team even in difficult situations."

title: Kim Ji-won Focuses on Diverse Tosses to Outmaneuver Opponents - 조선일보
content: Setter Adapts to New Teammate, Aims for Unpredictable Offense “This was my first time winning a championship by actually playing in the matches. That’s why it felt so special.” Kim Ji-won, 25, the setter for GS Caltex in women’s volleyball, said she struggled to believe her team had truly won the championship even after clinching the title in last season’s finals. It was only after rewatching the match footage multiple times that she finally thought, “We really did win.” But now, she’s ready to put those sweet memories behind her. Meeting Kim at the team’s training camp in Hitachinaka, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan, on the 12th, she said, “I think we can’t afford to get too caught up in that anymore,” adding, “There’s a shared understanding within the team that we need to move on from last season’s victory quickly.” With the departure of Ahn Hye-jin, Kim’s responsibilities have grown heavier as she enters her seventh season in the V-League. She admitted that volleyball remains challenging, especially the role of a setter. Having played both attacker and setter in high school, she said, “If I had to pick the more physically demanding position, it would be attacker, but the one that makes my brain work harder is definitely setter,” adding, “Truthfully, setter isn’t a position where I get to shine.” Still, Kim feels the “joy of being a setter” when a ball she sets leads to a successful attack. She said, “When my toss forces the opponent’s blockers to commit only one player or leaves them completely unguarded, allowing the attacker to score, it’s incredibly thrilling.” This season brings another challenge: synchronizing with Tanacha Sutsot, the new Asian quota player from Thailand. While she’s grown so familiar with longtime teammate Gisele Silva that they rarely need words, Tanacha is different. “Her playing style is something I’ve never encountered before, which makes it both fresh and a bit difficult,” Kim said. To adapt, Kim is increasing communication during practices. She listens to what height and speed of toss Tanacha prefers and experiments with different sets to find the right fit. This training camp in Japan is another opportunity for Kim’s growth. She said facing Japan’s fast and precise volleyball style gives her new inspiration. “Playing against Japanese teams is so fast-paced it feels overwhelming,” she said, “But once I adapt to that speed, I feel like I’ve grown. Japanese setters are so skilled—there’s a lot to learn.” GS Caltex hired two Japanese coaches this season, including Suguru Ishii, who specializes in setters. Kim said, “He’s really fun normally, but turns completely serious during training,” adding, “I thought he’d talk about toss control after yesterday’s session, but he pointed out that my play was rushing because the opponents’ pace was so fast. His ability to see the bigger picture and give advice was impressive.” GS Caltex acquired Park Sa-rang, a 177 cm tall setter from SOOP, via trade on September 4. With new competition, Kim cited her unshakable personality as her strength. Her personal goal for this season is clear: showing fans she’s improved from last year. She especially wants to hear, “Her play has become more diverse.” For the past three seasons, Silva has scored over 1,000 points each season, making her GS Caltex’s cornerstone attacker. Kim’s task is to utilize Silva effectively while diversifying the offensive routes. “We can’t just rely on Silva,” she said, “I want to use all our attackers evenly and make our volleyball unpredictable for opponents.”

title: Oh Se-yeon Targets Quick Attack Improvement for GS Caltex - 조선일보
content: Middle blocker aims to boost blocking and quick attacks after championship win Until middle school, volleyball was merely a sport I watched on TV. I fell in love with volleyball while watching the 2016 Rio Olympics and later pursued a player’s path during high school. Though my start was much later than my peers, I am now preparing for my seventh professional season. Last season, I also contributed significantly to GS Caltex’s championship finals victory. Oh Se-yeon, 24 years old, who was interviewed at the GS Caltex training camp in Hitachinaka, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan on the 12th, said, “Since I started volleyball late—a fact I cannot change—I try to compensate by working harder on my weaknesses.” Last season’s championship held special meaning for Oh Se-yeon. In her debut season, GS Caltex achieved a treble by winning the KOVO Cup, regular league, and championship finals, but she was mostly on the sidelines then. Oh Se-yeon remarked, “Winning by actually playing last season made it feel more valuable.” The most memorable match was the third game of the championship finals. She recorded eight blocks, lifting her team to the top. Oh Se-yeon smiled and said, “That day, the opponent’s attacks were strangely visible.” As a middle blocker, Oh Se-yeon is not particularly tall at 180 cm, but she compensates with her long arms and jumping ability. She explained, “Since my jumping is decent, I am confident in side blocking while moving. However, quick attack blocking requires jumping in place, which I still find challenging. It’s an area I need to improve.” Now in her seventh professional season, the biggest weapon Oh Se-yeon aims to reclaim this season is blocking. Compared to the 2024-2025 season—her first as a starter—she felt her blocking performance last season was unsatisfactory. She receives detailed guidance from head coach Lee Young-taek, a former middle blocker. Oh Se-yeon said, “When blocking, my hands tend to fall back, so the coach often advises me to push them forward more. I’m also practicing to time my quick attacks and maintain proper form even when my balance is disrupted.” She is equally eager to improve her quick attacks. Last season, GS Caltex heavily relied on Gisele Silva in attacks. If middle blockers actively engage in central attacks, they can distract opponents’ blockers and reduce pressure on Silva. Oh Se-yeon stated, “If I score more attack points, opponents will struggle to focus solely on Silva. This year, I want to increase my quick attacks.”

title: The Buick Muscle Sleeper That Ran With Chevelles For Half The Price Today - HotCars
content: Subscribe to the HotCars newsletter to never miss an update You'll kick yourself for missing this undervalued Buick muscle car that terrorized Chevelle models at the drag strip. It’s an overlooked high-performance bargain you can scoop up for a fraction of the cost. It outsmarted rivals back in the day by dodging high insurance premiums, making it an excellent buy. Now it continues its legacy by outsmarting collectors, hiding in plain sight as buyers spend excessive amounts on more expensive models with similar power under different badges. Born in 1991, I missed the muscle car glory days, but I've spent time discussing sleeper options to make up for it. The point is that for decades people have described Buick as a brand for older buyers. The brand is also described as incredibly luxurious, with refined models appealing to an older demographic. In the 1960s, Buick wanted to shake its reputation as a luxury brand for older buyers by breaking into the booming muscle car market. To attract younger buyers instead of families, it decided to take a swing at rivals like the Pontiac GTO and Chevelle SS by launching a high-performance line. This effort involved keeping prices low to compete while producing enough raw power to challenge the competition. So, a massive big-block V8 engine was stuffed under the hood of a smaller, lightweight frame to gain authentic street credibility while maintaining upscale comfort that it already had a reputation for. Some will say the Buick’s swing missed and failed as the muscle car project didn’t last long. However, Buick is one of the prominent historic brands that still survives today, while Pontiac was retired long ago. But Buick still has the same reputation for building comfortable grocery haulers as its classic muscle car goes unnoticed. The Grand Sport has entered the conversation. The 1968-1969 Buick GS 400 is a serious contender with a 400 cubic-inch (6.5-liter) big-block V8 that’s factory-rated at 340 horsepower and 440 lb-ft of torque. It can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in about 6.5 seconds and complete a quarter mile in roughly 15.2 seconds at 92 mph with a top speed of around 130 mph. The 1968 Pontiac GTO 400 H.O. can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in around 6.4 seconds with a 14.2-second quarter-mile time at roughly 98 mph with a top speed of 126 mph. Then the Chevelle SS 396 accelerates from 0 to 60 mph in about 6.5 seconds and eats a quarter mile in around 14.4 seconds at 105 mph with a top speed of 130 mph. The Buick GS 400 rides on the redesigned A-Body platform with a 112-inch wheelbase and features an aggressive semi-fastback roofline paired with an S-shaped sweep spear sideline. The engine features a 4.04 x 3.90-inch bore and stroke, a 10.25:1 compression ratio, and hydraulic lifters. It breathes through a 750-CFM Rochester four-barrel carburetor, two-inch intake valves, and 1.62-inch exhaust valves with a dual exhaust. The Stage 1 package boosts power to 350 hp. It includes a camshaft upgrade, heavy-duty valve springs, a higher-pressure 60 PSI oil pump, and performance carburetion/transmission tuning. The 1968 Buick GS 400 had an original price of about $2,926 for the hardtop coupe, while the convertible started at around $3,271. Meanwhile, the 1968 Chevelle SS started at around $3,100, and the Pontiac GTO 400 H.O. started at $3,101. It was competitively priced and managed to avoid higher insurance premiums by having a conservative look that didn't draw attention. Its sophisticated style was part of the problem; the Chevelle SS and Pontiac GTO had much bolder styles with stripes, aggressive fender lines, and high-performance visual cues to attract younger buyers. Other muscle cars projected a stripped-down street performance attitude that was in high demand. Names like Chevelle and GTO were already more established as popular muscle car nameplates, while Buick carried an upscale, family-car reputation. Buick maintained a traditional advertising approach while Chevrolet and Pontiac actively marketed to younger buyers in the racing and pop culture scenes. The Buick GS 400 was famously “fast with class,” which appealed to those looking for more comfort instead of a stripped-down, brawling nature. It features deep-twist carpeting, wood-grain accents, plush bucket seats, an upscale instrument cluster with a tachometer, and other luxury appointments. But unfortunately, it faced much lower sales than its rivals. People passed on the Buick GS 400 in the late 1960s, and many still don't know what they're missing today. It’s more affordable than rivals despite being much rarer. In 1969, the Chevelle SS 396 sold roughly 90,000 units, while the GS 400 moved about 1,256 hardtop coupes and 212 convertibles equipped with the Stage 1 package. The value of the Buick GS 400 in average condition starts around $17,400. Models that have been well maintained typically sell for closer to $32,500. Convertible models in show quality will cross the auction block for up to $65,000. A few extremely high-profile examples have eclipsed the $80,000 mark. Meanwhile, the 1969 Chevy Chevelle SS 396 starts at about $20,000 for models in rough condition. Examples that are in good driving condition will sell for between $50,000 and $60,000. Then models in pristine condition fetch between $65,000 and over $100,000. Convertibles attract the highest premiums. The 1969 Pontiac GTO 400 H.O. Ram Air III fetches between $79,000 and $110,000, while the Ram Air IV hardtop models sell for between $150,000 and over $250,000. Judge and convertible options will fly past $600,000. The Buick GS 400 is well worth considering as an affordable way to enter the market, offering a unique style and plenty of power while saving thousands. We want to hear from you. title: This Citroen GS Concept Isn't Real, Unfortunately, and It Dwells Across Some Parallel CGI Universes - autoevolution
content:
Citroen introduced the iconic DS model in 1955, and it became an even more luxurious executive car compared to the innovative Traction Avant, so it had a sizeable gap in the model range between the cheap Ami and 2CV models and the luxurious DS around the 1970s. That need for a bridge among them was filled by the Citroen GS in 1970, and the car immediately won the European Car of the Year for 1971, mostly thanks to its DS-inspired and technologically advanced design, the class-leading comfort and safety, plus the aerodynamic body. It also had an instantly-recognizable four-door fastback silhouette which was carried on by its successors, the cheap ZX and the more upscale BX. The model was produced in places like Chile, Indonesia, Mozambique, Portugal and Spain, South Africa, Yugoslavia or Thailand, in addition to France, thus cementing a cult status place in global, not just European, automotive culture. So, are we surprised that folks continue to remember it, even some four decades after its retirement? More precisely, this time around we’re dealing with a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI - Mike G., the leader of the 'mike.g.concepts' design studio, "fueled by adrenaline and innovation," has reworked the classic Citroen GS/GSA into a modern EV, aiming to take advantage of Citroen’s legacy and of Stellantis’ propensity for all-electric powertrains. The author’s Citroen GS/GSA concept “transforms the original’s famous aerodynamic silhouette into an exercise in modern minimalism” as he uses “crisp” LED accents, the iconic and comfortable hydropneumatic ride, and an ultra-quiet electric powertrain, seeking to use the design study to “bridge the gap between classic French avant-garde heritage and the future of sustainable mobility.” All in all, it’s now a bad attempt: the silhouette is instantly recognizable due to the four-door fastback profile, the LED headlights have the same form as the ones on the original but with modern light elements, there are slim exterior mirror cameras, and the triangle-shaped taillights also get modern LED touches. The nods to the past continue with the semi-covered rear wheels and the form of the doors. Inside, the concept is pretty simple: there’s blue leather everywhere with chrome trim and white piping; the iconic one-arm steering wheel makes a comeback despite having an integrated airbag, and the dashboard recalls the GS and GSA but with modern digital instrumentation. So, what do you think – yay or nay?
